title: Personality - 1. Bridging Psychology's Foundations
content: why personality and its transformations? because people are something, and they're also becoming something. And if you want to understand personality, you have to understand it as a state and as a transformative process. And of those two, probably the transformative process is most relevant because the transformative process is essentially equivalent to consciousness. And there's nothing that's more emblematic of what a human being is than the process of consciousness. personality and its transformations. State and process. Why a clinical introduction? some people who teach personality are also social psychologists and a smaller minority are clinical psychologists. And I'm a clinical psychologist. And I got interested in personality through clinical psychology rather than the reverse. I'm interested in understanding personality as it pertains to mental health or even flourishing, as opposed to psychopathology and the hell that accompanies mental illness. And that's the rationale for the clinical approach. And that means that what we'll cover in some ways is more theoretical than might be the case for people who are trained more purely empirically or from the social perspective. I'm very interested in the philosophical approaches— religious and philosophical approaches to personality, as as the scientific approaches, and I think they're reconcilable. one of the experiences you might have if you train as a clinical psychologist is going to be, depending on the school that you attend, is that the psychoanalytic types, who are increasingly rare, are set against the behaviorist and more physiological types, or vice versa. The behaviorists are set against the psychoanalysts, but from my perspective, they're just viewing the same set of phenomena from different perspectives. And one of the things that I'm going to help you appreciate is the hierarchical nature of personality, the fact that it can be analyzed at multiple levels, that there's some apparent internal contradiction, depending on where you start, depending at what level at which you approach the problem, but that those contradictions are more apparent than real. I'll endeavor to provide you with something approximating a coherent and complete description of personality lacking in detail, as all forms of knowledge are, but one that will allow you to reconcile the findings of the more empirical biologists, and behaviorists, with the more abstract psychoanalytic thinkers and the phenomenologists. I believe that they, all those levels of analysis have their utility. And to the degree that they're correct, they're not going to be fundamentally disunited. Assuming that there's something coherent about both personality and the approaches to personality, and there is something coherent. It took me a long time in teaching and thinking to start to understand not only how the theories differed, the multiple theories that we'll discuss, but what was the same about them, which is, I suppose, equivalent to something like the core of personality theory. And that's a very, very exciting thing to understand, because everything that you'll learn in this course, I will endeavor to make directly, personally relevant to you. It shouldn't ever devolve into a collection of dead facts. This is something you always want to do. If you're lecturing in a manner that is actually compelling, the material has to be accurate. factually accurate, but it also has to be relevant to the people who are listening, because otherwise they'll, their attention will wander and they won't remember. And you'll bore yourself and your audience. And that's never a sign that you're on the right track, . All right, what are we going to cover? Seven different domains in an introductory manner. Because this is an introductory course. We're going to talk first about religious and mythological conceptualizations of personality and its transformations. I like to set the more recent, psychoanalytic traditions and everything that stemmed forward from that, including the behavioral traditions, in a much more broad historical context. I think that's necessary, partly because you don't want to suffer from the delusion that everything about human beings that's relevant and accurate has been discovered in the last 150 years, which is most definitely and absolutely not the case. The scientific understanding of personality and the clinical understanding of personality have a deep affinity with markedly traditional understandings of the nature of human beings, stemming all the way back, as we'll see, to the shamanic conceptualizations, which are, in all likelihood, hundreds of thousands of years old. Modern human beings, in our current genetic form, emerged about 350,000 years ago. We can assume some continuity of conception and process over that entire period of time, and that's also something extremely interesting to know as setting yourself in a historical context that's that archaic, gives you a much more fundamental sense of who you are and where you came from. And it's also the case that understanding those extremely archaic ideas, which also tend to be very fundamental and unchanging, sheds substantive light on many of the things that you'll experience in the modern world, most particularly the meaning of the narratives, the fictional representations, the movies and dramas that grip your imagination and entertain you. There's a reason that a fictional representation is entertaining when it's of high quality. And the reason is, is that it echoes in your soul, to speak, at a very, very deep level. And one of the things that you'll come to understand more deeply, I hope, in consequence of this course, is why that echoing occurs. Then we'll talk about the psychoanalytic tradition. Now, the more strictly scientific types tend to be skeptical of the analytic tradition, and that's a big mistake. It's partly because the scientific enterprise actually has a number of stages, and one stage is scientific hypothesis testing and data analysis. Careful experimental analysis. The behaviorist types, who are pretty physically grounded, were very good at that end of the scientific enterprise, as were the psychometricians who concentrated on the measurement of personality. But the psychoanalysts, the psychoanalysts were exceptionally good at generating hypotheses, and that's a more unexamined part of the scientific tradition. Where do ideas come from? How do you generate an idea that's innovated, innovative and interesting? And the, Freud and Jung, and their associates and followers were unbelievably innovative in their approach to conceptualizations of the human mind. And I would also say that recent developments, especially with regards to large language models and artificial intelligence, have demonstrated, I believe conclusively, that the psychoanalysts were exactly on the right track in relationship to the structure of the human unconscious, and we'll go into that in some detail. And that's something very new. I've only been able to understand that relationship in the last two years, because the large language models have really only been on the scene for that length of time. I think large language model cognition can help us understand what the psychoanalysts meant, technically meant, by symbol. Now, one of the reasons the behaviorists who are more down to earth, have criticized the psychoanalysts, literary critics, for that matter, is their claim that the interpretations laid out by people like Freud and Jung were nothing but projections of the imagination. They bore no relationship to reality, no demonstrable relationship to reality. But the large language model calculations are predicated on the idea in a way that every word or every idea is surrounded by a cloud of ideas that are highly likely to co-occur together statistically. Right, you could imagine that the word witch, for example, is quite likely to be accompanied by words like cauldron or coven, and very unlikely to be surrounded by words like skyscraper or stainless steel, and that a given concept exists within a cloud of associated conceptions. And the elaboration of that cloud of associated conceptualizations is something like the symbolic analysis, the free-association symbolic analysis, of the psychoanalysts, and also of the symbolic investigation of the literary critics. I suspect we're on the cusp, in the realm of artificial intelligence, of mathematically systematizing our assessment of symbolic representations. I already have a large language model built that's predicated on my work that's very good at dream analysis. And that means to me, and I think this will happen, that the analysis of dream images will become something that can be purely scientific and mathematically encapsulated. and I think, I really believe that psychoanalysts, starting with Freud, were on the right track conceptually and practically with regards to the investigation of the symbolic meaning of dreams and literature for that matter, drama. that's extremely exciting. The idea that we can make a, not only a science, but even a mathematical model of the symbolic landscape that we inhabit. we'll delve into that in some detail. Carl Rogers and the humanists. The humanist tradition is, I think it's a secularization of Christianity, essentially. Carl Rogers himself was a, was a missionary before he lost his religious faith. And his representation of human personality and psychotherapy, because Rogers was very involved in the psychotherapeutic tradition, is a recasting of the Christian idea of redemption into the realm of secular mental health and psychopathology. Rogers believed that truth-seeking in the psychotherapeutic process was intrinsically redemptive, which is a restatement, of the gospel notion that the truth will set you free. We'll delve into Rogers analyzing, in particular, his conception of dialogue as transformative, and do our best to understand what that means practically, with regard to your relationship with yourself, but also to other people, and also what it means in relationship to the genesis of psychopathology and its cure. Existentialism and phenomenology. The existentialists, the Freudians, the Freudians made the essential presumption that the trauma was the cause of much psychopathology. That the default human personality was healthy. But when it suffered damage, especially early in life, the healthy developmental path was circumvented and various forms of pathology emerged. The existentialists questioned that particular Freudian presumption, making the case instead, which is also a case grounded in deep religious tradition, that the vagaries of human existence are such that suffering capable of generating psychopathology is not necessarily a consequence of trauma, but built into the structure of human existence itself, not least because we're self-conscious, say, and aware of our own mortality, which is an existential problem of sufficient magnitude to give us all grounds for a certain degree of mental illness, and perhaps even malevolence in the absence of any particular marked trauma. Which is not to say that some people don't have it worse than others, or that you won't have it worse at some times in your life than others, and you will. It's not to say as that the consequences of having it worse might not have some additional influence, on you, on your, the course of the development of your personality. I really like the existentialist approach, because I think that the notion that the, the problem that—what would you say? Mental health problems, to speak, the problem of psychopathology is not a consequence of the deviation of the normative or ideal human pathway, but something that's baked into the structure of human existence itself, that we all have to grapple with the finitude of our existence, and our subjugation to suffering. And that understanding that, how that warps and dements us, and also how that might be dealt with in a forthright manner, is of great utility. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, who's not precisely a personality theorist in the classical sense, although is definitely an existentialist, made the case that the lies attendant on the human proclivity to deny the existential reality of our own experience not only warped our souls in the most profound of ways, but also laid the groundwork for the development of the terrible atrocity-seeking totalitarian states that most particularly characterized the 20th century. And the other great contribution of the existential theorists, as far as I'm concerned, is their ability to link the inadequacy of any given individual's approach to the existential problems of their own life with the emergence of something like state-sponsored hell on Earth. And I think that that's something of absolutely crucial significance to understand. There's probably, one of the cliches that emerged in the aftermath of the Holocaust in World War II, or prior to World War II, prior and during, prior to and during World War II, was the notion that we should never forget what happened. But you can't remember something you don't understand. And it's not particularly easy to derive the lesson from Auschwitz. Now the existentialists and again, I would say particularly Solzhenitsyn, went further and Viktor Frankl went further along that path than anyone else trying to draw a relationship between your individual moral obligations, your failure to live up to them, and the genesis of the authoritarian catastrophes that characterized the secular 20th century. The phenomenologists I find particularly interesting because they, following Heidegger, approached the problem of what constitutes reality in a very unique manner. The more scientifically-oriented Enlightenment behaviorist types and the psychometricians make the assumption that the most appropriate way to conceptualize reality, the truest way of conceptualizing reality, is in relationship to its objective truth. Now, there's some problems with that presumption in that our experience of reality, which in some complex way is indistinguishable from reality itself, has an irreducibly subjective element which the objective tradition has a very difficult time dealing with. The phenomenologists attempted to circumvent that subjective-objective dichotomy by describing reality itself as that which is experienced, and adopting that approach. first of all, profoundly transforms the manner in which you think about what constitutes the real. If you assume, consciously or implicitly, that only objective, that only the objective is real, you cast your own emotions, motivational states and dreams, fantasies, visions of the future, even the meaning of your life, into something that constitutes some second-order reality or even a non-reality, and that has potentially devastating, that contributes in a potentially devastating way to the development of a life-devouring nihilism. If you're nothing but a brief flicker of flame, no, composed of dust on a third-rate planet at the edge of a minor galaxy, it's very easy to become cynical and dismissive about the fact of existence itself and your own life. And reconstituting your idea of what constitutes reality to, on the assumption that what you experience is the most foundational, is the, is the fundament and the foundation, transfigures the manner in which you might conceptualize the dignity and significance of your own existence. And that's a crucial, that's crucial existentially, because if you have contempt for yourself, as a second-order reality, that's, it's very easy for that to become contempt for other people and even contempt for existence itself. And that's a very dangerous road to walk down. And one whose nature has been laid out quite comprehensively in the religious and mythological representations of man and woman that we already discussed and in the psychoanalytic and existential traditions. the analysis of the phenomenological approach, which puts human experience at the center of things, or maybe even experience itself, or maybe even conscious experience itself, is a powerful antidote to that dehumanizing objectivism, . And Heidegger himself formulated his philosophy, upon which the phenomenological approach was predicated, in order to combat that dehumanization and then paradoxically fell prey to the Nazi ideology and, say, degenerated into a supporter of precisely the psychopathological approach that he in principle was attempting to fight. ironic twist in 20th-century history. The Piagetian tradition. Jean Piaget, a developmental psychologist, not often regarded as a personality theorist. But that's generally because personality theorists don't know how to integrate his thinking into the personality tradition. And I think I know how to do that, and that's not a problem. I like Piaget and thought a lot, not least because it points, and he knew this to something approximating an emergent morality that has a certain grounding in objective, in the objective. Piaget noted, and we'll delve into this, in some detail, that the games that children spontaneously play have a particular pattern. part of that pattern would be, if I force you to play, that's not a game. And I'm not going to be a popular child, and you're going to be a bitter and resentful kid in consequence of the force and compulsion that's been applied to you. A game, a true game, has to be voluntary, has to have rules that both parties accept and are willing to abide by. There's only a set, there's a pattern, to games that have that quality and that can be played sustainably or that can be played in an improving manner. And the essence of the set of all playable games that can be played in an improvable manner is the foundation of morality. There's a very important thing to understand. You see that importance of that make itself manifest in the stages of childhood, where children start to become truly social, which starts to emerge around the age of three when they can begin to take the perspective of someone else, when they begin to have true friends, when they can engage in reciprocally altruistic behavior, when they can take turns and share, right—which is to learn, to begin to learn, how to treat another person as if they had the same status and importance as themselves or their own desires. That capability, developed, makes them highly socialized, popular, and happy children, and also turns them into the kinds of adults who can engage in sustainable and improving patterns of cooperative and competitive behavior with other people, which is a good way, for example, of conceptualizing a friendship or a marriage. It's a game that can iterate, repeat. It has a certain pattern and the iteration produces improvement as it progresses. Now, you could imagine that there's many ways of interacting with people that do not have that property, and a small subset, a straight and narrow path, that characterizes the set of interactions that do have that property. And if the goal is voluntarily sustained improvement of function, socially distributed, that's not much different than the establishment of a transcendent ethic, the transcendent ethic upon which morality itself might be predicated. And that's a very useful and interesting thing to understand. it's a great antidote to the idiot moral relativism that proclaims that all approaches to social interaction are of equal, are diverse first in their essence and also of equivalent value. Because there's no transcendent ethic, no possibility of a transcendent ethic. I think that's mostly just an escape from fundamental responsibility rather than an intelligent approach. But I also think that the Piagetian analysis of the emergence of games in children, which you could dismiss if you were casual in your thinking as something relatively trivial— why be interested in the games that children play before they're mature? His analysis of what children are doing is profound that it points the way to the reconciliation between the religious viewpoint and the scientific viewpoint, which was actually what Piaget was trying to do. That was his motivation. And that's really something to understand as . I also like the Piagetian tradition because it builds the—it allows for the comprehension of personality from the bottom up, to speak. Piaget was interested, for example, in what he called the basic reflexes that children bring into the, that infants bring into the world when they're born. The micro movements and preconceptions that they're capable of manifesting, upon which the entire superstructure of socialized personality is erected. It's a bottom-up approach, and one of the things that's lovely about that, from a philosophical perspective, is that it maps extremely onto the neurobiology of the brain and the development and maturation of those neurobiological structures in the course of human socialization. And we'll move from the Piagetian tradition to the biological talk about the physical foundations of the motivational and emotional systems in particular, although also the perceptions and patterns of action that characterize us as biological entities, and we'll do what we can to integrate that biological view with the religious tradition, the analytic tradition, the humanistic tradition, the existentialists and the phenomenologists, the Piagetian developmental constructivists. And then finally we'll close with the psychometric approach, which concentrates on the science of measurement and the use primarily of statistics to lay out the domain of human personality. The most effective psychometric, psychometrically oriented psychologists have identified six, seven—it depends on how you break them up—fundamental human traits. One is general cognitive ability, which is likely the most—what would you say? It's the most powerful abstracted conceptualization of the entire corpus of social science and medicine. There's nothing that's more documented, easier to measure, and more powerful and reliable as a conception and predictor than psychometric intelligence. And there's nothing more controversial and potentially cultural, culture-destroying. The culture war that besets us is in no small part an emergent consequence of the findings of the psychometricians, particularly on the intelligence side. It's a brutal, bloody business. One of the things you learn as a clinician, especially if you do IQ testing, is the absolute scope of the intellectual differences between people. They're stunning. And given that there's no better predictor of long-term life success than psychometric intelligence, there's no better predictor of climbing, the economic ladder. There's no better marker of future success at birth than intelligence, including wealth. The differences between people in intelligence are pervasive and marked and also very fundamentally, biologically predicated, which is also an awful realization because we like to believe as, what would you say, compassionate people committed to the notion of equality, that everyone can learn equally, and that the field of opportunity, especially with regards to complex matters, is open to all. And there is very little evidence that that's true. one of the most damning statistics, for example, which we will refer to further, is the fact that the US Armed Forces, which has been using psychometric tests continually since World War I, when they were trying to determine how to organize people rapidly to fight off the threat that the war constituted, they turned to psychometric testing, which was developed by French psychologists and perfected to some degree by the English, especially the socialists, as it turns out. They turned to psychometric testing to identify potentially promising officers and continued their investigations into psychometric measurement for 60 years, concluding, I believe, by the 1980s, something like that, 1990s perhaps, that no one with an IQ of less than 83 could be trained under any circumstances whatsoever to do anything that wasn't positively counterproductive while they were members of the Armed Forces. And that is really something to understand, given that that's about 10% of the population, and that the Armed Forces is always desperate for manpower and committed to using a career in the Armed Forces as a stepping stone for people, in the underclass or in the working class, to move themselves up the economic hierarchy. they're highly, highly motivated to make use of everyone available and yet concluded after their 50-year investigation that 10% of the population cannot be utilized in any productive manner whatsoever for military enterprises. And it doesn't take much thought about that to understand that something approximating the same thing applies in the general world, which means that the conservative idea that everyone can get ahead merely as a consequence of diligent effort, and the liberal idea that everyone can be trained to do anything given enough resources, are both seriously wrong, and nobody knows what to do about that. now the psychometricians also outlined the basic structure of personality considered from a statistical perspective, generating the now -known -called Big Five models—extraversion, neuroticism, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness. Honesty, humility is sometimes added to that, as is the Dark Tetrad, which is a constellation of malevolent and counterproductive personality traits. We'll analyze all the five traits, broken down each into their two aspects. We'll start with religious and mythological conceptualizations to provide this historical context. as I mentioned earlier, human beings of our type took our form, something approximating, 350,000 years ago. Because there's not a lot of evidence for rapid cultural progression until something approximating 20,000 years ago. Something like that. I studied the most archaic personality conceptualizations, including conceptualizations of transformation, primarily by investigating the writings of Mircea Eliade, who was a Romanian historian of religions and a true genius. He was someone who basically operated in something approximating the psychoanalytic tradition. He was a compatriot of Jung, for example, of Carl Jung, whose school was influenced heavily by Freud, and Eliade was very interested in the universal patterning of religious ideation across cultures. He's a theorist who was cast aside by the Postmodernists, who now dominate the universities and certainly the field of inquiry into the history of religious ideas, because the Postmodernists claim— this is the fundamental Postmodernist claim— that there is no fundamental uniting metanarrative. And that's a critique, an extended quasi-Nietzschean critique, of the idea of God, a continuation of the death of God that Nietzsche famously pronounced, but also the insistence that there is no fundamental unity that aggregates our personalities, within ourselves or across people—a very dismal and disenchanting view of human nature. If you are not particularly amenable to conflict, because if there's no fundamental unity, then there's a fundamental disunity, and if there's nothing but a fundamental disunity, there's no integration of personality and there's no hope for peace. Now, the way the Postmodernists dealt with that existential problem was by—what would you say? Surreptitiously inserting a uniting metanarrative derived from the Marxists, which is the narrative of power and the presumption that the only game in town is my attempt to attain dominance and status, likely or even inevitably, at your expense, that there's no such thing as genuine dialogue. For example, there's no discussion between people of intrinsic worth and goodwill oriented towards establishing something like a maintainable peace, which would imply a unity. There is only instead something like the Hobbesian war of everyone against everyone. That's a world predicated on power. And I believe, speaking psychoanalytically, that people who believe that are doing it primarily because they want a justification for using nothing but power. And I also not only believe but think, I know that a world that's predicated on nothing but power is indistinguishable from the total—the atrocity-committing totalitarian states of the 20th century. Now, I had a discussion at one point with Camille Paglia, who's a very -known literary critic, and she said something very interesting that's relevant to this course, something I'd never heard any other psychologically-oriented thinker state, which was that, if the academy, the universities, particularly the departments of English and their literary critics, had turned to the school that Eliade was part of, that included Erich Neumann and Carl Jung, for example, many other thinkers, particularly of the Bollingen School, the history of the last 30 years, particularly with regards to the culture war, would have been entirely different. But if you do it, if you leap to the solution, not least because you're impatient, with the wandering, good for you, except you've solved the wrong problem, and that's not going to be very helpful. And it's a painful thing. Make no mistake. This is a painful process because if I have a problem, if we have a relationship, if I have a problem, you might be the problem. And one of the things that I'm going to explore is, is it you? Now, if I'm honest, I'm also going to see if it's me with equal, what would you say, diligence. But during that exploratory process, especially if it's a serious problem, a lot of things are going to come out of the woodwork. And you got to be patient. And same applies if you're a practicing psychotherapist. See, Freud figured this out. We'll turn to that in the next lecture. This is why Freud developed the free association process. His approach was, say whatever comes to mind, whatever, whatever. Now, people rarely have an opportunity to do that. If someone listens to you, which almost never happens, you get to say whatever comes to mind. Now, Freud noted that that's actually a process, and that process unfolds in a manner that descends, takes apart, and then reconstitutes. He got that right, as far as I'm concerned. And that makes sense, right? Because imagine that your attention wanders as you speak. Something appears to you and then something else appears to you. All you have to do is think about that for 15 seconds from an evolutionary perspective, say, and you'd understand that that's obviously purposeful. Freud's observation was that if you just listen to people, their speech will wander until it finds a problem, and then it'll circulate around the problem and descend into it. And then, possibly, with all the destruction that entails, also generate a solution. And one of the things that almost all therapists figure out is that sometimes someone will have a problem. They bring it to you, and what the solution is. But if you tell them, it's useless, partly because they don't know the details of the solution. But even more importantly, because they didn't come up with it. And they haven't thought it through. They don't even really know why they should implement it. It's not like you can give someone their destiny as a gift. They have to do the hard work. And if you're interested in practicing as a therapist, or training as a therapist, one of the things you really have to understand is there's almost nothing you can do that's more effective than just listening. Just listen. You have no idea how many people there are out there, perhaps including you, who have never been listened to by anyone in their life and who are, in consequence, full of knots that haven't been untied and stories that haven't been told and realizations that haven't made themselves manifest and intuitions that died stillborn. It's not good. But the other thing, too, is that that's a key to success. People will tell you what they want and need if you listen to them. They will tell you everything. It's a remarkable thing. They'll tell you things they've never told anyone else or even themselves, if you just listen. And what that means is that, if you learn to listen, then people will tell you how to deal with them. if you have a business and you actually listen to your customers, if you're fortunate enough to have customers, they'll tell you what you're doing right, and they'll tell you what you're doing wrong. And all you have to do is listen and do those things, and poof, you're successful. I spoke with the comedian Jimmy Carr about how he prepares his comedy routines. Many comedians do this. When they're preparing a new tour, that they take out into the world, their 90-minute routine, they go to small clubs and they try out their idiot jokes. And some of them aren't funny. No one laughs. Some of them, people laugh. they just overproduce. That's Darwinian. Overproduction. Then they test and they cull everything that isn't funny and they keep what everyone laughs at. And once they have 90 minutes of things that everybody thinks are funny, because they've been told that, they go on the road and everyone laughs. And you can't believe how much that's the secret to life. when you talk about voluntary versus involuntary, how does the trope of the reluctant hero fit in with that? when Pinocchio first encounters Monstro in the abyss, he turns tail and runs. That's a very, very common mythological motif. And that's because the thing you're avoiding is worse in its essence than you think. And by the time you discover that, it might be too late. You'll be tempted to run. Very, very common reaction of the reluctant hero, who then, inevitably, insofar as he's a hero, reconstitutes himself and goes forward. Maybe he gathers more resources. Maybe he gathers more allies, maybe he, what would you say, engages in the proper sacrifice. In some manner, he fortifies himself, and likely by making reference to his aim. When Abraham is called by God to undertake the adventure of his life, he undergoes a sequence of transformations, and each is marked by a sacrifice. Part of what the sacrifice is, is he builds an altar to reorient himself towards what's highest, to remind himself that's what he's doing. And you need to do this periodically in your life. You undertake a particular task, and then the task comes to an end. then what? that's like a little fragment of your personality has made itself fully manifest. Now what? the answer to that question is, you interact with what's highest, once again, in the abstract sense, and wait for the next revelation forward. What should I do next? it depends on what you're aiming at. But you're aiming upward. You wait for the pathway demarcated by that aim to make itself manifest again. And that is how your perceptions work, . This is something absolutely crucial to understand. And I think it's an unassailable fact. The pathway for—your perception is primarily of a pathway forward. Pathway forward with obstacles and facilitators, a pathway with friends and foes, a pathway with agents of magical transformation. That's the landscape of the world. The pathway forward that reveals itself is dependent on your aim. Now, there's nothing that should terrify you more than that realization. Because what it means is that the world's reality makes itself manifest to you, both perceptually, at the level of fact, and emotionally, in absolute lockstep with your aim. Jung said, you better bloody know what your aim is. That's Jung's injunction to understand the story that constitutes your life. Because unbeknownst to you, you might be playing a very pathological game, which is very unlikely to end for you or anyone else. That's the unconscious grip of an underlying pathological narrative. You live in a story. You might not know what the story is. You probably want to learn what it is. Jung, for example, pointed out, like the psychoanalysts were wont to do, that many people live out the unlived wishes of their parents. That's the story they're encapsulated in, right? Or maybe they're the targets of their parents' hatred and vengeance, and they carry that burden their whole life. And that's the story that structures their existence and within which their emotions operate. What's the story? That's the fundamental question. That's part of what we're investigating, a large part of what we're investigating in this course. Another question? You briefly touched on objective and subjective reality when you talked about Heidegger and phenomenology. I wanted to know, how do you balance those two things in a concise way? That's a good question. You do that in part by watching your effect on others. I mean, part of the reason that it's useful and necessary to surround yourself with other people intimately is that the people around you give you a slap when you've deviated too insanely from the proper straight and narrow path. You might think, and the psychoanalysts are probably, and some of the other clinical psychologists, are probably to blame for this, that you're mentally healthy if your psyche is arranged properly. And that is one way of looking at it. But really, a more accurate way of looking at it is that you're saying, if you've been socialized enough that other people can stand having you around, and then all you have to do is surround yourself with other people, and every time you're too dim-witted, they'll just give you a slap. And then you outsource the problem of maintaining your sanity. And if you're tilted too far towards your own subjectivity, your friends, if they're friends, are going to start poking at you with increasingly rough jokes, for example, or your wife is going to turn away from you, or your relationship with your children is going to start to suffer. And you can watch and listen. This is also what great leaders do, . They watch and they listen, and then people tell them what their problems are, and then they can figure out how to solve them. That's a great technique if you want to run a family or a life or your business or a country. And that's the logos in dialogos, is that if you pay attention to what other people are telling you, bounded by tradition, as we pointed out, then you don't have to be that wise. You just have to adjust when necessary. You'll hit the straight and narrow path aided by the others who hopefully have your best interests in mind. It's also useful, and I think not only your right, but your responsibility, to surround yourself with people who are on the side of your better angels. Often people don't understand that they have that right, is that if people are pulling you down, walk away. That's even what's best for them, because someone who's trying to pull you down, who is facilitated in that endeavor, fails to learn that that's not acceptable behavior, and it's seriously not acceptable behavior. You referenced personal variables like IQ and interest, which we can't control. Do those variables impact our individual ability to transform? And if what does that tell us about predestination and individual control? That's a hard question. That's two hard questions. There's no correlation between intelligence and morality, as far as we can tell. No correlation with agreeableness or disagreeableness. Both those could be elements of morality. No correlation with conscientiousness. intelligence probably has something to do more with the, what would you say? The rate of possible transformation, both positively and negatively. Remember Lucifer. Lucifer is the archetype of the intellect who worships itself. And he is the worst of all subterranean spirits. And that seems to me to be part of the way that the cosmic balance is, what would you say, established and maintained. You might be given the talent of an IQ of 145, but that comes with its requisite temptation, which is to presume that you're smart enough to determine the course of the moral order itself, which is Eve's sin and Adam's sin and the sin of every totalitarian everywhere, always. And there is a predestinarian element in a sense, but maybe in no more a sense than we walk with two legs. There are principles that govern our existence, and some of those principles are the talents that we've been given rather than earned. In the Gospels, part of the explanation for that is that from those to whom much has been given, much will be demanded. And the idea is that, if you are rewarded in a particular way by some stellar trait, that you have a responsibility that, if you don't shoulder, will crush you. And Christ says in the gospel of Thomas that what remains unrevealed within yourself will destroy you. And that's a hell of a thing to understand, too. if you are a genius, and that's God-given, biologically instantiated, which is really what the evidence suggests, then you better use that properly and not take undue pride in it, or it'll be an enemy of yours brutal you can hardly possibly imagine it.

title: Personality - 3. Navigating the Unconscious
content: All right, everyone. this is the analytic tradition, the psychoanalytic tradition. And we'll concentrate primarily on the originator of that tradition, one Sigmund Freud, and also his most brilliant colleague, Carl Jung, who extended and, I think, improved Freud's magnificent contribution. Freud is a very popular whipping boy these days, perhaps especially among more behaviorally oriented psychologists. But that's partly because almost all the truly brilliant things that Freud discovered are much now part and parcel of what people take for granted that only the places he was wrong still show up. Now, there isn't anyone in the modern world who's even vaguely educated, who doesn't take the idea of something approximating the unconscious as a given. to a large degree, we owe that to Freud. And if that was his only contribution, that would be remarkable, a remarkable contribution. It's by no means his only contribution. Now, one of the ways of understanding the psychoanalysts is, as I mentioned in the first lecture, you can think about the human personality as a hierarchically tiered structure, which is the same, as its representation in the nervous system. And there are approaches you can take that are from the top. We seem to be organized at the top of our personality, at the highest strata, according to something approximating a story. Whereas at the bottom, in the micro details, we're organized according to microactions. My ability to do this, trivial as it is in a sense, is, what would you say, is the most differentiated sub-element of my personality. If my personality is expressed in actions, that's the expression of all these motor movements that I'm capable of manifesting. And my personality can emerge upward out of the body, in its actions, or it can emerge, it can be analyzed from the top down, taking into account the broadest patterns of my life. The psychoanalysts started from the top down. Behavior therapists, and then in psychoanalytic treatment, the psychoanalysts aim often at a radical restructuring of the personality. And sometimes that can happen when you make a particularly profound realization in your life. The behaviorist types, they usually start from the other perspective, which is, is there something small that you can do on a daily basis that would incrementally improve you, that would lead to an expanding transformation of your ability, your productive ability, and your ability to function in the world across time? Both of those approaches work. I would say for the typical person, because I was trained as a behaviorist and I knew the psychoanalytic tradition, I had the option with my clients of either approaching them from a behavioral perspective or a psychoanalytic perspective. Almost inevitably, for the, most commonly, I would start with the behavioral approach. It's simpler. But I had people for whom the psychoanalytic approach was more appropriate. They were usually people who are more creative and who are capable of and interested in the investigation of ideas and also in the possibility of dramatic and revolutionary transformation. there are people for whom that's more suitable. I suspect, as I said before, that the clients that Carl Jung attracted were like that because he was known for his interest in religious ideas and philosophy and attracted creative people. And they're capable of and interested in revolutionary personality transformations for the typical person. And this is not a value judgment for the typical person. An incremental practical approach is more understandable, more desirable, and easier to implement. But that doesn't mean that the psychoanalysts had it wrong. And there's many things they had right, very right, very seriously right, and we'll investigate some of them. To understand Freud, it's useful to understand something of his historical background, the time. the first thing we should understand, because Freud is often dismissed with regards to his hypothetically patriarchal views, which I think is really one of the stupidest generic criticisms that can be leveled at anybody of thought whatsoever. It's just an excuse for not paying attention to the details. You can find the odd misogynist thing, for example, at least apparently misogynist, that Friedrich Nietzsche said in the corpus, immense corpus, of his writings—the same with Freud. And if you're inclined, you can throw out the baby with the bathwater as a mere consequence of that. But it's really not that bright. The devil's in the details. And thinkers as profound as Freud and Nietzsche, it's very difficult to derive the true benefit from their work, merely in consequence of an overview, and very dangerous to dismiss the, what would you say, the body of work because some part of it displeases you. First of all, you might ask yourself why it displeases you, because it might be you and not the author. Walking through the actual writings is extremely useful. In any case, Freud did live in a society where the divisions between the sexes were much stricter and harsher than they are now. And that was partly because all protestations about the evil patriarchy, notwithstanding, was primarily because birth control was unreliable. And the fact, the pill, it's almost impossible to overstate how dramatic a revolution the birth control pill actually constituted. Because before that, the idea of equality between men and women, that was just an impossibility, fundamentally, for practical reasons as as philosophical reasons, . We also, modern people, we're daft. We don't understand how much of the fact that men and women can basically play on an equal footing now is a consequence of things that we just take for granted, like the existence of plumbing everywhere. That did more to emancipate. Plumbers did more to emancipate women than all the philosophers in the history of the world. And it's also the same thing, the same is true of the peace that reigns on our streets. Historically, it was almost impossible for women in many societies ever to go anywhere at all without someone masculine and powerful right by their side. And there's plenty of places in the world where that's still true, because a woman alone was a target for any exploitation imaginable. And that's not the case in the West. And that's because we've spent an awful lot of time civilizing ourselves. And it's been very, very successful. And now we take that for granted, and that's not wise. The sex rules in Victorian England were quite differentiated, and the issue of sex was already somewhat complex because of that and because of the lack of reliable birth control. But there was another factor that also made the Victorians a more repressive society, which is relevant to why Freud, for example, was convinced that repression, per se, was at the heart of psychopathology. Syphilis was a terrible plague in Victorian England. The evidence is that syphilis came to Europe from the New World. Mostly, Europeans exported the worst possible diseases to the New World. Mumps, measles, smallpox killed 95% of the native North and South Americans, even before the Puritans landed, 95%, maybe more. The North Americans returned the favor most effectively in the form of syphilis, which was a terrible plague and could also be transmitted from parent to child, from mother to child. And it manifested itself in a plethora of symptoms, very difficult to accurately diagnose and almost impossible to treat, plus a disease with devastating and terrible degenerative neurological consequences, followed by death. And the Victorians had their reasons to be uneasy on the sexual front. And that's all background for Freud. I think this is from Henri Ellenberger, who is a French-Canadian existential psychologist who wrote a great book called The Discovery of the Unconscious. And if you want to know as much as you could possibly know about the psychoanalytic tradition and its history in one book, The Discovery of the Unconscious is the right book. It's a great book. Remarkable work of scholarship. And he does a wonderful job of detailing out the thought of Freud and Jung and of Adler, who we won't talk much about, Alfred Adler, as as detailing the history of the idea of the unconscious before Freud formalized it, because there was much speculation about the unconscious before Freud's synthesis, and exposition of the idea in a most fundamental way. Freud also belonged to what Ellenberger described as that "unmasking trend, the search for hidden unconscious or implicit motivations characteristic of the 1880s and 1890s. In Freud, as in Nietzsche, words and deeds are viewed as manifestations of unconscious motivations, mainly of instincts and conflicts of instincts." That's a different way of looking at the world than the Enlightenment view or the rationalist view, which would presume that the fundamental drivers of your utterances and conceptions are your attempts to rationally understand the world. The psychoanalysts, beginning with Nietzsche—this is a more romantic philosophical trend—insisted instead that your words and thoughts are often handmaidens of your emotions and motivations and, therefore, expressions of your deepest instincts. Now, I think those views can be reconciled in that, if your words are only the handmaidens of a motivation, then you are immature and driven or even possessed. If your words and utterances are a consequence of the integration of your motivations and emotions at the highest possible level, then you're rational and mature. And the rationalists are accurate in their claims that people are rational when they're talking about mature and integrated people, but completely inaccurate when they're talking about people whose personalities, people whose personalities are fragmented or who have remained immature. And we know this in part because of our analysis, of the brain physiology, but also of cortical maturation. When you're born, you're born in a semi-developed state, especially cortically. A baby is mostly subcortical function. That doesn't have any bearing on whether or not infants are conscious, because consciousness is a very, very old phenomenon. It's not dependent on the cortex. in fact, if you take a cat and you take out all of its brain except the hypothalamus, which is just a little cap on the spinal cord, like 90% of its brain, it's hyper-alert and hyper-exploratory. That's pretty weird. The less brain a cat has, the more awake it is. Right? Weird. a lot of the brain is inhibitory. A lot of it, especially at its higher levels. It's regulating the expression of underlying motivational states. Now, when a child emerges into the world, parts of it, parts of that person, are wired up. The child's mouth and tongue, for example, are already fully functional, which is why children will mouth everything, but also how they manage to latch onto the nipple and not die. And the child myelinates from the mouth outward and from the center of the body outward, developing the more sophisticated and environmentally specific adaptations that will enable them to function in the particular environment at hand. That's all associated with the maturation of the cortex. The child comes into the world with certain reflex functions, which we can describe, certain nascent abilities that can expand, but also with a set of a priori motivations and emotions. with infants, for example, rage is very common. when infants, for example, develop stranger anxiety and cry when someone other than their mother comes into the room, it's not because they're sad, it's because they're enraged that it wasn't their mother who showed up. And that was discovered by people using a man named Paul Ekman's schema of facial emotional coding. you can code the position of muscles in a manner that reliably indicates the underlying emotion and infer, for example, with infants. And if you're around infants at all, you can tell the difference between an anger cry, which is usually, the infant is usually red-faced and the cry is quite penetrating and, what else would you say? angry, if you listen to it properly. People can't listen properly because they never think their infant could be enraged because they're cute. It's like, no, no, they're completely possessed by rage, 100%, like a toddler having a tantrum, holding his breath till he turns blue and passes out. Try that. See if you can do it. It's quite the manifestation of instinct. And children, this is one of the things that's fascinating about children, is they cycle through basic motivational and emotional states. They're in one 100%, and then they're in another 100%. They laugh, and then all of a sudden they're crying, then they're hungry, and then they want to play. And it's quite an exciting thing to observe, and it's very dynamic and alive. But there's no higher-order integration of those lower-order motivational and emotional states. It's just now, they're in the now completely. And there is something to be said for being in the now, to be engaged like that. But as a medium- to long-term survival strategy, it's not sufficient, which is why you don't see autonomous bands of two-year-olds roving successfully through the woods. You can't rely on your underlying immature emotional and motivational states to orient you in the world. That also speaks of something we alluded to earlier, which is the idea that there is an emergent ethic that's something approximating universal. You can't survive if you're run only by the short-term demands of your emotions and motivations. That has to be not much repressed or even inhibited in the Freudian superego sense, which we'll discuss, but more like integrated into a pattern of attention and action that does, in fact, satisfy those emotions and motivations, but does not at the expense of other people and in a manner that ensures the viability of the future as as the present. And you can imagine that the cortex is necessary to manage that computation in any given unique human environment, and that it takes a long time for a child to learn how to regulate their behavior other people like them, which is really quite something to manage and also very useful, and also that they regulate their behavior, their present actions don't interfere with their future viability. That's something like delay of gratification, . The capacity for long-term planning, the capacity to engage in effortful work. And that's the opposite of immaturity. Nietzsche and Freud pointed to the fact that words and thoughts were not the rational, the manifestations of the underlying rationality that the Enlightenment types presumed was part and parcel of the human psyche, that they could instead be nothing but the verbalizations of underlying emotions and motivations. If you're talking to someone who's immature and manipulative, you run into that right away. They're always after something with their words. And it isn't peace, and it's not the ability, the willingness to reconcile in a cooperative and productive way. It's not playful. It's an attempt to do what a two-year-old does, which is to get what they want with their words now. And that's not a pleasant person to be around for any length of time. anyways, it seems like there's a parallel pattern between cortical maturation, and the emergence of a viable sustaining psychological and social ethos. And it makes sense because how could it be otherwise? It's like, you mature, you put all that effort into maturing, and it signifies nothing and it's pointless? That makes no sense whatsoever. There's a point to the painful process of learning to regulate yourself. It's also interesting and worthy of note that immature people tend to identify with those motivational and emotional states that possess them. Because the question might be, to someone, I want this. Nietzsche would object, and Freud perhaps too, that no, something within you wants that you identify with. And that's not the same thing at all. if you're under the influence, of aggression or sexual compulsion, you can identify with that urge and make the presumption that that's you. But Freud, and even more particularly Nietzsche, would say, why is that you rather than the you that's the force that's, say, trying to regulate your aggression, or trying to integrate or trying to be playful with other people? just because a want emerges doesn't mean you're that want. Right. This is something I think is particularly relevant to the current culture war, because part of the expression of the culture war is the insistence of radically immature and hedonistically possessed people, that their essential self is nothing other than their sexual desire, which is just not a viable identity, as you can tell by the eternal fragmentation of identity in the West. "In Freud, as in Nietzsche, words and deeds are viewed as manifestations of unconscious motivations, mainly of instincts and conflicts of instincts. For both men, the unconscious," the unconscious would be the domain of the instinctual motivations and emotions in this regard. "The unconscious is the realm of the wild, brutish instincts that cannot find permissible outlets, derived from earlier stages of the individual and of mankind and find expression in passion, dreams, and mental illnesses." that's one definition of the unconscious, which is, that's like the id as definition, right? It's the, what would you say? It's the operation of the instinctual within. And then Freud's point would be that instinctual operation can also become perverse. Imagine that sexuality or aggression, because those are the two drives, to speak, subpersonalities, really, that Freud was most particularly concerned with—those are difficult motivations to integrate into a personality, not least because other people object to your aggression, and they may object to your sexual desires as . And it's a very tricky problem indeed to allow those proclivities to find their expression, but also to do that in a civilized, socialized manner that allows other people to play along voluntarily. High order of demand, and that can easily go wrong. And Freud's observation, and Nietzsche's, was that fundamental motivational states whose expression are blocked tend to become pathological devils in very short order. And that's very much worth considering virtually forever. And it's another example of that rule that we discussed in lecture one. If you're gifted with a great intellect, for example, and you take inappropriate pride in it, or you don't carry the responsibility that's attendant upon it, it'll turn against you. And the same is true—this is Freud's fundamental realization, I think—the same is true of any of the fundamental motivational states that are part and parcel of your biological makeup. If you can't determine how to conduct yourself that those drives, subpersonalities, are satisfied, they will become your enemies and the enemies of other people, and very powerful enemies indeed. Now, as Ellenberger alludes to here, too, Freud also noted, and I believe this is accurate, is that these underlying motivational states that can't find expression in a socialized and acceptable manner do tend to make themselves manifest in fantasies and dreams. Now, you can understand this quite rapidly if you watch yourself, which is something that the psychoanalysts would recommend. for example, if you're at work and you're frustrated, especially if you've been frustrated repeatedly, there will be fantasies of revenge that flash through your mind, and they're really waking dreams. You can catch the images if you watch. Now, Freud would say you're likely to repress them because you like to think better of yourself. But if you watch, you can see that, and you can play with it. You can even allow it to possess you. If you're angry, there'll be a fantasy that goes along with that. Now, it's very useful to allow that fantasy to make itself manifest, because then you can find out what you're up to. Now, maybe you don't want to be up to that, but your anger might have something to say. Maybe you're being bullied at work. Maybe you're not standing up for yourself properly. Maybe you have a tyrant that's ruling you, and you should do something about that. And maybe that's true of your life in general, because you're a pushover. And the vengeful fantasies that your aggression will produce are also guidelines to the pathway of adaptation that should characterize your forward movement. That's part of that integration of the shadow that we talked about. Same is true on the sexual front. One of the things that bedevils people in their marriages is their unwillingness to admit to themselves what it is that they want, sexually, and certainly their unwillingness to communicate to their partner. men, for example, might harbor the fantasy of their virginal, morally pure wife, which is a lovely fantasy in a sense, but very difficult to reconcile with, the deepest reaches of sexual desire. And men of that sort will unconsciously, implicitly, punish their wives for any manifestation of the sexual desire that they would actually like to have happen, and deprive themselves and her of the sexual adventures they might have if they were both more honest with one another. And it's very useful. This is that shadow analysis. It's very useful to observe what the darker parts of you want because, not least because the part of you that is uncomfortable with such things might be exactly the moral coward who's pretending to be moral instead of—the coward who's pretending to be moral in the Nietzschean terminology, rather than the person who's actually good because they're absent of aggression or inappropriate sexual desire. Not wise. Much better to put it on the table and figure out what to do with it than to pretend it isn't there. Living things, including parts of yourself that you tend to extirpate, tend to become very annoyed about that and seek for their revenge. And that's not pretty. It's seriously not pretty. that'll express itself—this is Freud's observation—in increasingly pathological, fantasies of aggression, revenge, and sexual conduct. And I think Freud was right in his emphasis on sexuality and aggression, because those are the two fundamental motivational systems most difficult to integrate into socialized being. They're very primordial, too, both sexual desire and aggression. Especially defensive and predatory aggression are instantiated at very low levels of the nervous system because amphibians have sexual behavior and aggression. I mean, we share the neurological systems with animals way back in the evolutionary chain. And you mess with those, you fail to make those deep-level impulses manifest at your peril and the peril of others. "Even the term id," the 'it', because that's what id means, "originates from Nietzsche." Freud thought of the id as, what would you say, nature operating within you. And you can think about this, anger is a good pathway to that conceptualization. I'm angry, but it's more accurate to say, anger possesses me. And it's more accurate to note that the anger that possesses you is not even actually human, not fundamentally, because have you ever seen an angry dog? Anger is a motivational state that's fundamental that it transcends the merely human. And when anger possesses you, you are giving rise to the expression of something that's stunningly primordial and ancient. And it's very useful to understand that more even as a state of possession rather than a drive. The behavioral types tended to think of motivational states as drives that made you operate algorithmically or in a rule-bound way under their influence. But that's not accurate. If you're angry, you see the world through angry eyes. Your perceptions themselves are transformed by that motivational state. this because sometimes you'll have an argument with someone you love. And while you're angry in the argument, possessed by that desire to win, all you can see about that person, even though you love them, is everything about them that's not good, which you'll inform them about and remember. And even the memories that come to mind will be specific to your, anger-induced desire to win and to defeat. These underlying motivational systems are personalities. They're subpersonalities, uni-dimensional subpersonalities, that possess your perceptions, your speech, your memories, as as your actions. They're not just drives. They're better conceptualized as living forces that are partly you and seriously partly not. That's partly why they're expressed in archaic societies, in particular as deities, right? Like eros.
