To put your CV together, you have to put your past together. And maybe that takes two years. If you want to find a job you actually like, two years isn't too much of an investment to make. And maybe you're terrified because you're going to throw your CV out in the wind and 49 out of 50 times it's going to be rejected. But then you could look at it actuarily and presume, of course that's the case, because lots of companies advertise positions that don't even exist because they want to keep a continual flow of CVs going through the system, or they advertise because they're required to legally and they already have a candidate, or it could be that, at this particular moment, you're not the best candidate for that particular— there are a lot of reasons why you're not going to get the job, but they're true for virtually everyone. And when that the base rate for CV submission failure is 95%, then you don't have to take it personally. And you can think, "I need a new job. I have to send out." you ask yourself, how many bloody resumes can you stand to send out a week? And that's a serious question, right? How much disappointment can you take? I don't know. Maybe you can handle 20 and maybe you can handle 5. There's going to be some individual difference in that, but you could consult yourself and find out. And maybe you're afraid to begin with that you can only send out one. It's like, one is a lot more than zero. And once you've done one, maybe you could do three. And once you did three, maybe you could do 10. And you could settle on, I'll send out— you make a routine out of it. I'll send out 10 resumes a week for, like, a year. And if you do that, if you've updated your CV and you're aiming at jobs that are hypothetically within your purview, and you have a good story to tell about why you would be the right candidate, and you can figure that out, too. If you have a good story to tell, you're not going to be nervous about telling it. you got to ask yourself, why should someone hire you? And then you've got to discuss that with someone, your wife or friends, and have them hammer away at you until what you have to offer. And then you can go in there with a bit of confidence and you can say, "I don't know much. I don't have any experience in this realm, but here's a bunch of things that I've done. And here's the investigations that I've made about your company. And this is why I think I'd be a good fit, and this is what I can offer to you. And I won't be a catastrophe," which is the one thing everyone hiring really wants to know. It's like, what do you think? Can we do this together? And if you have an attitude like that, and you do get an interview, which you will eventually, then the probability that you'll get the job has gone up substantively. And you don't have to stay in your damn rut, but you do have to figure out what elements of what you don't understand, that chaos and potential, are terrifying you into paralysis. And then you think, "I'm terrified into paralysis by the magnitude of the job search." It's like, fair enough. You may have lots of things that you have to put right. Make a list of all the things that frighten you, right? Maybe it's 15 things. Then you can rank-order the list. This frightens me the least. Maybe I could try it. And if all of the things frighten you too much you're paralyzed, break them down. When I was counseling my clients to go on the job search, one of their first assignments was often "just open up your CV and look at it." And this was an actual contract, because when you're playing this game with yourself, you can't cheat. If you're terrified to go on the job search and you've motivated yourself enough that you're willing to open your damn computer and look through your CV, don't sit down right then and start rewriting it. It's a violation of the contract. You're pushing yourself too hard. What you should do instead is give yourself a little pat in the back and say, "sad as it is, I was terrified to do this, but I did it." Right. it's time to, like— if you have a child and the child does something new, you're not going to say to them, if you have any sense, "Why didn't you do twice as much?" That's a great way to demoralize someone. You also shouldn't do that to yourself. If you've taken a step forward, like, have a little recognition, and maybe you've got someone around you, if you're lucky, that you could tell what you did to, and they would be happy about it. And that's how you distinguish, between the people you should have around you and the people you shouldn't. Because if you have people around you, and you tell them that you made a small step forward, and they make light of it or are cynical about it or punish you for it, you might think very hard about just who it is that you're hanging around. Because you want to be with people who note your progress forward and at least don't get in the way. And that includes yourself, that's for sure. All right. there may be some cleaning up of the chaos in your past you have to do. And you can note that. Imagine you have a goal, getting a new job, and you see that there are obstacles in your path that are preventing you from moving forward. And then you see that some of those obstacles have to do with the past. then you have to clean up the past to the point where those obstacles disappear, and then you may find some obstacles in the present. Maybe you don't think you're good at interviews. Lots of people feel that way. then you have to practice that. That's a present problem, . And although it may have its roots in the past, maybe you're not sophisticated enough to conduct yourself in a job interview, but that's something you can learn. Write down 40 questions that you think you might be asked. Come up with an answer, not a lie, but an answer. Here's the problem with lying. you lie your way into a job. then you didn't get the job. The lie got the job. And if you had to lie to get the job, probably it's not the job for you. then your reward is that you get a job that isn't for you and that you don't deserve. that's a hell of a way to start a job. Why don't you start a job that is for you, that you do deserve, that you could do. That'd be a lot better plan. And I have to get a pretty dismal job given my qualifications. It's like, you start where you are or you start on a falsehood. And one of the things, there's this phenomenon in economics called the Matthew principle, . And the Matthew principle is, "To those who have everything, more will be given. And from those who have nothing, everything will be taken." And this is a reflection of a phenomenon called the Pareto distribution. And the Pareto distribution works like this: progress is not linear. It's geometric or exponential. Once you start accruing money, the probability that you'll accrue more starts to increase. This is why a very small percentage of the people have all the money. If you have a million, it's hard to make— if you have no money, it's hard to make a dollar. If you have a million, it's a lot easier to make the next million than it is to make the first million. And that continues. If you have 400 million, it's a lot easier to make a billion, et cetera. This is true, for every domain of accomplishment. Once you've recorded one album, it's much easier to record the next than it was to record the first. And the third is even easier than the second. Success builds upon itself. And what that means, and this is a good thing to know, as I said before, even if you have to start slow, that doesn't mean you're doomed to slow. And even if you have to take a job that's beneath you— which is not a good way of conceptualizing it, ; if it's actually matched to your talents, you should be grateful for it— if you do a stellar job at that job, the probability that someone will notice and push you along is extremely high. This is something also that people who are bitter and hold back don't understand. I used to get undergraduates come to work with me in my lab, and I had a lot fewer positions than there were inquiring undergraduates, right? they were high-demand positions. And generally, what I would do was give the undergraduate who's asking a task, a real one, because I'd have some—maybe I needed them to go investigate some psychological phenomenon, make me a little report about it, a research review, and I'd give them that obligation or opportunity. if you are talking with someone who has resources that you might want access to, if they ask you to do something, that's not an obligation. That's an opportunity. And if you have the two things confused, you're doomed. If you regard the things that will move you forward as an obligation, how in the world are you going to move forward? what would happen inevitably is that some of the undergraduates would go and do just a stellar job, and it would be done in two days. And then others would come back to me a week later and say, "all these things came up and I couldn't do it." And often the story was very plausible, because they had family trouble. I don't know what the hell the problem was. It was some real problem, or maybe not, but at least it sounded like a real problem. But then I'd go ask the people who did it, who actually did the job, and they had just as many problems. They just didn't let the problem stop them from doing the job. And then I would hire the undergraduates who actually did the job and not hire the undergraduates who didn't do the job. And "that's pretty mean because those poor people had problems." It's like, maybe they had problems, and maybe they were a problem. And one of the things I noticed was that if I pulled people into my lab who were a problem, that was a problem. And it wasn't just a problem that I had to deal with. It was a problem that often infected the entire lab and especially demoralized the people who were doing a good job. Right. And if you have to start where you are and you're grateful for the opportunity and you make the proper sacrifices and you work, then anyone with any sense will notice that. And anyone you want to work for has enough sense to notice when you're doing a good job. Now, if you're in a job where you're doing a good job and no one is noticing, you should ask yourself two questions. Do the people that you're working for know that you're doing a good job? Because it's possible that you're doing things efficiently that you're invisible and you're not very good at self-promotion, which is actually just communication. If you're doing a good job for people, they need to know it. And one of the times that you can inform them about that is when you go ask for a raise or a promotion. You need a little list. "Here's a bunch of things I did that made your life a hell of a lot easier than it might have otherwise been, and perhaps more profitable," that you may not have even known about. "And if you produce an increment of salary of this magnitude or give me a bit more flexibility or a promotion or some other opportunity, here's a bunch of things I could do for you that would make your life even better." It's like, if you have that story and it's real, and you present that to your employer, and they don't go, "That sounds like a pretty damn good deal. Are you sure that raise is enough?", then maybe you should decide whether or not that's not the right place for you to be working. And before you do that, too, you might have already wanted to get your CV in order and to have started sending it out to see what market demand there is for your skills, you can tell your employer as that you have other offers that are pending. And then you put yourself in a pretty damn good bargaining position. Part of the reason, that women do not make as much money as men— it's one of many reasons— is that they're not as good as men at promoting their own accomplishments. It's part of being agreeable and higher in negative emotion. I saw this when I worked in civil service in Alberta, years ago, when I was a kid, 20 years old. I saw that the bureaucracy was basically run by 50-year-old women who did all the work, and all of that credit was taken by narcissists who pretended that it was them and took all the credit from the conscientious older women who were working. Right, an ugly situation. And you could lay that at the feet of the narcissists for being manipulative and psychopathic. But those women should have learned that doing a great job invisibly is not a very good strategy. People need to know. And that means you shouldn't be tooting your own horn constantly because that's just annoying. But it does mean that the people for whom you're doing a good job should know you're doing it. And you should also note how much reward you need for doing a good job. Because if you're doing a great job and no one ever notices, maybe you're conscientious enough that that'll be sufficiently motivating for you. But most of us would like to be rewarded for a job done on some schedule. That's something else you can negotiate with your wife, your husband, your kids. It's like, one of you in a marriage is going to cook. a little appreciation for that now and then tends to improve the quality of the meals, and the atmosphere around the table. One of the things you have to discover about yourself, and this is also part of developing a vision is, what's the reward schedule that's necessary for you? And none, that's not a good reward schedule. And it's something to discover, right? Maybe someone only has to say something positive to you once every month. Who knows? Or maybe it's twice a day. There's going to be some temperamental variability that characterizes you in that regard. You're probably going to need to be rewarded more for things that you're just trying as . But this is a good thing to meditate on. How much notice do you need when you're doing something good? And this is something to negotiate with your partner. When you do something for them, you can teach them to notice it, and you can also let them know what they need to say. This is something else that's useful to know. Say you're having a dispute with your wife, and she wanted you to say something other than what you said. Now, that's what she's going to let first of all. "I would like you to say something other than what you just said." "What do you want me to say?" then she's going to say, "if you loved me, you'd know." Everyone laughs when I make that joke. Yeah, it's too vague. It's like, "No, I want to know exactly what you would want me to say. If I could say to you what would make you happiest, what would that be?" Now you're in trouble because you have to figure that out. Then you have to reveal that. Then you're going to be annoyed because you're going to say, "that's not genuine." It's like, yeah, maybe it won't be the first 20 times. But maybe the person can get good at it, and by the 50th compliment, not only will have the words right, but they'll also have the sentiment right. You have to let people be stupid about how they're treating you to begin with. The other thing you can notice, too, is that if your partner does do something that you really appreciated, something small and subtle, they sneak something good in just to see what might happen, if you're smart enough to jump on that, and you have to not be too resentful about their existence to do this, if you're smart enough to jump on that and say, "Ha, I saw what you did. This is how you greeted me when I came home. I got a hug, for example, instead of an immediate litany of never-ending complaints. That was a very lovely way to reenter the house." If you're very, very—this is something that's very useful with employees, too, and coworkers. If you see someone doing a good job and you say, "Hey, here's what you did," and you say it in detail, "I saw that and it was good," man, you do that a hundred times if you're running a restaurant, you do that to your employees, any of the employees worth keeping, they'll be working themselves to the bone to get another reward like that. People really like that. The Skinner, the Skinner behavioral psychologist, could train animals to do anything. He trained pigeons to guide guided missiles over enemy territory by pecking on photographs. That's hard. Skinner noticed that reward was the most effective form of behavioral transformation, but it was subtle, because to reward an animal for doing something you want it to do, you have to wait around until it does the thing, and then you have to reward them. And this is the same in your household. If you're watching your kids, maybe your kid by accident cleaned something up one day. You can notice that. You say, look, maybe they're five. "That was the thing an eight-year-old would do. Good work, kid. Here's what you did." They'll smile like mad. And the probability that they'll do something like that again radically magnifies. And kids are very good at generalizing, too. not only will they do that thing again, but they'll do things in that category again. And that's a fun way of interacting with people in your family, because targeted reward is a pleasure to give and also to receive. And it's a great way of establishing harmony in your household without the scraps, the fights that might otherwise be necessary. Sometimes you have to settle something, and that requires dredging up all sorts of things that everyone perhaps would rather leave buried, and attempting to sort through them. That's quite demanding. But targeted reward requires attention, but it's extremely effective and it's a very pleasant thing to engage in. All right, there may be things in your present that you have to sort out. Maybe you have to find your damn CV on your computer. Even that can be a nightmare. One of the things I saw with my particularly disorganized clients was that I'd ask them to get their CV off their computer, and then maybe they'd bring their laptop in, and the whole bloody thing was just a catastrophic mess. There were files everywhere. The computer hard drive was a reflection of their psyche. Everything was everywhere, and all that was valuable was lost. And maybe one of the things that, the first thing you have to encounter when you try to open your CV is the fact that your computer is such a bloody mess that you can't find anything. Imagine that, just imagine that. someone's in a job they hate. And in order to fix that, they have to sort out their CV. And to do that, they have to find it. And to do that, they have to confront their computer, which isn't that big a dragon. It's not nothing, but it's not cancer. It's trouble. But then that's annoying and embarrassing. And instead of doing that, they don't do it. And then they have the job they hate for 30 years. Right. Yeah. Not smart. And you could also see that there's a certain humility involved in noticing that your failure to confront the mess on your computer might end your life. Right.

content: It doesn't matter where you encounter chaos. It just matters that you do encounter it. And that's also a good thing to know. And what that means is that wherever you decide to take a step into the unknown, that's as good a step as any other place. I'll tell you a story about that. when King Arthur is sitting around the round table with his knights, they all go off to look for the Holy Grail. And the Holy Grail, it's like the promised land, right? It's like the kingdom of heaven. It's some item of infinite worth that exists out there, hypothetically. No one knows where. Technically, the Holy Grail was either the cup that Christ used at the Last Supper or the cup that caught his blood when he was speared during the crucifixion. it's the container of the holy liquid or the water that revivifies. That's a good way of thinking about it. The knights have no idea where to go to look for the Holy Grail because, first of all, they don't even know if it still exists. And even if it does exist, they don't know where it is. Now, they're sitting at a round table which implies that they're equals. Each knight goes into the forest at the point that looks darkest to him. That's a very interesting thing to know. There's a domain of chaos and potential that's part of your life. And there's going to be entry points that frighten you. It doesn't matter which entry point you take. It's all leading to the same destination. And that's another thing to understand when you're trying to overcome the shame you might feel when you note how small the step forward is that you have to take. But if you understand that it doesn't matter because you're confronting—no matter where you confront the dragon of chaos, it's the same dragon. Now, that's metaphysical and speculative. I'll say, no, actually, we know this, and here's how we know it. One of the things that therapists learned over the last 100 years, they learned that one of the things you do in therapy is you get people to tell the truth. That's a form of confrontation with the unknown. Because people will recite their story, and if they trust you, they'll recite it in a manner that they may have never managed before. They'll tell the truth about events, they have to trust you. That's a form of confrontation. Helping people get their story straight is part of what—that's their vision, of past, present, and future. That's one of the things you do in the therapeutic context, and that works very . It's a form of exposure to what's unknown. If I walk you through something terrible that happened to you in the past, you might cry. It might distress you a lot. When you first tell the story, you're going to be all over the place. It's going to pull in all sorts of terrible things that happened to you. Once you tell the story and then you retell, it's how it's going to be much shorter and much more focused. If you continue doing that, you'll eventually get to the point where it's summed up by your conclusion. Then that whole bloody mess is going to be replaced by a marker that you can now use to step forward. This is a good thing to know, too. If you're listening to your partner, and this is particularly true of men who are listening to women, women are more threat-sensitive than men. That means they'll bring up more issues. The threat-sensitivity that women bring to bear on a situation is instinctual rather than cognitive. And what that means is, they know something's up, but they don't know what it is. And that means that you have to listen to them wander around. And now, as a man, your proclivity is going to be, "Tell me the bloody problem I can fix it," which is really what you're being asked to do. But the problem with that response is, there's no sense fixing the wrong problem. Something you have to learn as a diagnostician, if you're a physician or a psychologist, too. You have to let people talk long enough you actually know what's wrong with them. That can take a long time. If you're listening to someone who's upset, they're going to wander around because they don't necessarily know why they're upset, and they're going to stumble upon a bunch of things they think they might be upset about, and some of those might be you. And that's annoying. But you have to let the wandering occur until the person gets to the point. And when they get to the point, usually what happens is, the point is actually smaller than the whole domain of problems, and then it's something that you can address. And it's the same thing if you're bothered. You can leap to the problem-solving stage rapidly, or you can do some investigation and try to figure out just exactly what the hell is it that's stopping you. That's a question you can ask yourself. One of the purposes of meditation and prayer, the purpose of thought for that matter, thought is a secular form of prayer—if something's bothering you, you can ask yourself, this is a meditative exercise, what is it that's bothering me? It's a question, but you have to want to know the answer. And that's frightening because maybe the thing that's bothering you is trivial, but probably not. It's probably connected in some way with something that really bothers you. It's the same idea that every window into chaos is a window into the same thing. Something that bothers you will be emblematic of all things that bother you. they're frightening to investigate. But if you're willing to open yourself up, you'll see that fantasies will enter the theater of your imagination about what it is that might be bothering you. Maybe you're irritated at your boss. The first—why am I irritated at my boss? What would I like to do? First fantasies that come up might be quite aggressive and violent, especially if you're very annoyed. But your imagination will start to toy with the possibility of providing an answer to the question that you posited. If you are careful and you want the answer, you will circle around the thing that's bothering until you get to the core. You can usually tell you've got to the core because you don't like the answer. It's a good hallmark of truth. It's like, oh my god, really? That? Then you probably got it. Yeah, and that's part of the humility. That admission is part of the humility that's necessary to move forward. In therapy, you often find that people are avoiding something. If someone has a panic disorder, anxiety disorder, and they're agoraphobic, maybe they're afraid of elevators. Then you can expose them in imagination or in reality to the elevator. Now, they're not afraid of the elevator, because who's afraid of an elevator? It's like, no one's afraid of an elevator. Then you find out about the fantasy, and the fantasy is almost always something like this. Person with panic disorder has had heart palpitations, and a lot of them, and they're afraid they're going to die of cardiac arrest, and they have reason to be afraid of that because a panic attack produces a radical acceleration of heart rate, especially if you have a family history of heart disease, and your dad dropped dead when he was 40, and you're terrified of anything that has to do with your heart. what you're afraid of is that you're going to go in the elevator, and your heart's going to act up, and there's going to be other people in the elevator. And then as you die, because you have this heart problem, you're going to make a fool of yourself. And that's the combination of the two things that are most frightening to people, like biological mortality and social exclusion. And the elevator becomes a place where that confrontation is likely. I had a client once, I got her right up to the doors of the elevator. We started quite a ways away. And when the doors opened, she said, "That's a tomb." That's right. Great Freudian symbolism in that because the elevator for her was a place of death. I think, "an elevator isn't a place of death." It can be. For her to go into the elevator was no different than her confronting the fear of death. I would say, too, when you discover an obstacle that's in your path, that's a severe obstacle, and you look into it, that's analogous in some profound manner to confronting the reality of your vulnerability per se. Now, the disadvantage of that is that even small things can stop you. But the advantage is that, if you are willing to voluntarily confront the small things that stand in your way, you're simultaneously confronting the entire domain of things that you might be afraid of. And what you see in psychotherapy, this was a revolutionary discovery because it wasn't what was predicted. When you encourage people to confront the small things that they're afraid of, they don't become less afraid of those things. You could think they become less afraid of the specific thing they're exposed to, but equally afraid of everything else. That isn't what happens. They don't become less afraid. They become braver. That's not the same thing. Less afraid means the thing isn't as threatening you thought. Braver means there's more to you than you realized. If you become braver and you realize that there's more to you than you realized, that you hadn't noticed because you were avoiding, then you can bring that to every situation. One of the things clinical psychologists noted was often women who were suffering from anxiety disorders who went through exposure therapy, they often ended up fighting with their husbands in the aftermath of the exposure therapy. It was because they got more assertive, because they were braver now in relationship to the things that were threatening them. They weren't dependent on their husband, which was usually the alternative. Sometimes people will develop panic disorder if they are dependent and a divorce is looming, because then they have to be alone. If you're dependent on someone else for your emotional stability, you're not going to bring up difficult issues with them because you're going to be afraid of breaking the security that the relationship, that the relationship constitutes. if you get braver, you think, "Now I got a few things to say to you." It's also the case, this is rather perverse, is that the husbands in that situation may have been working at counter purposes to their wives' development, knowing at some level that, if their wives got braver, they'd bring up all the dismal things about the relationship and them that need to be brought up, that they were covertly punishing their partner for being brave whenever, "No, dear, you don't have to do that. I know you're not feeling that today." It's like, that sounds like care. It's not care, or it isn't necessarily care. It can be the worst thing that happened to you. It's the same with kids, is that maybe the right answer to a kid who is wondering whether or not he has the wherewithal to do something is, "Get the hell out there and try it." Not, "Yeah, I understand you're not having a good day." There's a devouring element to that excess of care that, has all sorts of devious branches, let's put it that way. It's a good rule that people who care for the elderly use, . Don't ever do anything for anyone they can do themselves. You're stealing from them. You're not helping them. It's one of the things you learn as a therapist. You come see me. Those are your problems. They're not mine. Now, that enables me to listen to you because I won't take all the burden of your troubles on myself, and you won't have to feel guilty about that. But more to the point, I don't want to solve your problems. I want to help you solve your problems because then you get to have the gift of having solved your problems. That is not something you want to steal from people. If you're wondering as a mother why you have to let your kids suffer, it's like, it's you don't steal their destinies from them. All right, you have to map out your life, past, present, and future. Now, we generally assume that when you develop a vision, that the vision you're developing is oriented to the future. But if you develop a new conceptualization of who you could be in the future, it's highly probable that that's going to change the way that you conceptualize your past experiences and your present experiences. If you do something that radical, if you are learning, for example, how not to be bullied at work, your story about your past may have been "innocent victim constantly pursued by psychopathic narcissists," and perhaps that's 50% true. But if you learn that there are patterns of behavior that you're manifesting that are making that bullying more likely, the story is going to change about your past, which is weird because you'd think that the past is fixed. It's less fixed than you think, is that, I was bringing to bear certain inadequacies on my part that were drawing out the implicit bullies in people, even when that wasn't necessary. It means you're going to be taking some more responsibility for the past onto your shoulders, and that can be a real drag, especially if you had a lot of negative experiences. But if the consequences of that are that you've now paved the way forward to more future success, that seems like a small price to pay. There's an insistence in classic religious rituals. This is something deeply built into the Judeo-Christian substrate, for example, that you should confess and repent, that you should be, what would you say? You should bring your sins to mind. You can understand how that's burdensome. When I went to church, when I was a kid, 13, and the minister was always railing on about the intrinsic sinfulness of man, I would sit there and think, "God, I just don't think I'm doing things that are that bad," which, wasn't true. But I didn't get the point. The point was, you should try to figure out what you're doing wrong. Why? you can stop. And this is also something to know about your partner in marriage, too. If they're alerting you to insufficiencies, maybe that's because they're tyrannical narcissists and you should sort that out. But maybe they've got a point. And it's worthwhile delving in to see. It's like, what exactly are you telling me? Because it's going to come out as a vague accusation to begin with. I want to know exactly what your problem is. Then I want to know, is this your problem or is this my problem? If it's your problem, we're going to deal with that. If it's my problem, I'll deal with it, too. But I need to be convinced that it's my problem, and I need to know exactly how it's my problem. Now, why would I want to know that? if I have a problem, maybe I should fix it. One of the things that's happening in our culture is we continue to have arguments now about whether or not you're allowed to utter offensive truths. I would say any corrective truth is offensive. There's going to be stupid things about you that you're clinging to. Now, if you act them out, they're going to hurt you. It's a state of play, and the play is designed to facilitate the mutual development of the people who are inhabiting the relationship. This is another reason we get married. I mean, we already talked about the fact that it keeps the chaotic catastrophe of continual romantic entanglement at bay. You could think about that as a security-seeking strategy, but then there's more to it than that, too. if you love someone—generally, if you fall in love with someone, it's someone you respect and admire, and it's someone that you have, in that respect and admiration is, at least in principle, some regard for their ability to push back. Most people don't want to marry a doormat. That's part of the spirit of romantic attraction, to find someone like that you can play with. That's what little kids are practicing when they make cross-sex friends. You're doing exactly the same thing as when you're an adult, playing house, trying to construct with your wife or husband a shared vision. Here's a good way of thinking about that, too. One of the things I noticed in my clinical practice, again, was that, in a marriage, you need to spend about 90 minutes discussing the details of your mutual lives with your partner, practically. He's the person that people who are lost follow. he stands up against the tyrant and he frees people from slavery. Now they're near the end. They're on the border of the Promised Land. you could imagine now. Now, the Israelites are on the boundary, and is Moses, of the Promised Land. But they're still in the desert and they don't have any water. And they're bitching and squawking about the fact that they don't have any water and that they should have never left Egypt. And who the hell is Moses? And what's God up to? And the whole thing. Now, his staff is a symbol of tradition and authority. And his staff, imagine that you're the leader of a nomadic group and you have a staff, and someone's getting out of line. That's another way of thinking about it. Moses hits the rocks with his staff. And he does that twice, not once, twice. And God says, "Because you hit the rocks with your staff, instead of using your words, you do not get to enter the Promised Land." And that's a hell of a punishment for someone who spent 40 years leading a fractious group of slaves out of this dismal tyranny. The fact that he uses force at all when he could use invitation means that he doesn't get to his destination. Now, that's worth thinking about. In your own household, now and then, maybe your children are misbehaving badly that you have to use compulsion to rein them in. With your wife or your husband, if you have to use compulsion or deception or manipulation, instead of getting voluntary assent, you're never going to get to your goal. What you want to do, and this is a good thing to know, too, if you're running a business, for example, or you're trying to please your customers, is like, when I'm negotiating for a business deal, I'm never trying to figure out, "How can I get get the best deal?" Which would mean, I get a great deal and you don't get such a good deal. That's a stupid deal because, if you're too dumb to figure that out, then you're not going to be a very good business partner. If I did pull one over you, once you figure that out, you're not going to be very happy with me. If we're yoked together now because we're partners, and I took advantage of you as my first move and put you in a lower position, now you have to labor forward with that for decades, how is that going to work? How is that possibly going to work? It's the same thing. If you have to use manipulation or force to get assent from your wife for anything or from your husband, it's like, there may be times when you can't conceptualize any alternative, but it's a suboptimal solution and you will not get to where you're going if you use it. But what you'd really want, if you got it right, is to offer a solution that the other person was thrilled with. It's like, "Yeah, I'd really like that." Great. Why don't we aim at that? Why don't we aim at that? What we'd both really like to have happen. Sometimes, sometimes you can only do the best that you can do with what you've got. And plus, you can't fix it anyway, you might as go with that. content: All right. how else do we put up walls? We organize ourselves politically, right? And we have hierarchies of social organization that surround us. And we've figured out how to formalize that we can have conflicts and compete and cooperate without degenerating into absolute chaos. And then we also frame the world with our bodies. part of the way that we solve the problem of the fact that we're surrounded by an infinite amount of that which we do not understand is that we can't see that much. You hear what you hear, but not everything. And you see what you see, but by no means everything. What you focus on visually is a very, very tiny percentage of what you could conceivably see. You don't see what's behind you. You don't see what's to the side of you. If I'm looking at you, I'm not looking at you, right? even that focal perception restricts. Our bodies are—what did Huxley say? Who's the philosopher? I can't remember his name at the moment. Huxley wrote about this in The Doors of Perception, is that there's a world of infinite wonder around us all the time, but that infinite wonder is also overwhelming. And one of the things that being embodied does is restrict our view to the point where it's narrow enough that we can master it. You don't see more than you can understand, perhaps. It restricts it. And embodiment is another invisible frame. It excludes as much as it includes; it actually excludes more. And then there are sub-bodies, to speak, within us. And you could think about those as instincts. Your senses frame the world. you see the world visually, you hear the world, you touch the world, you taste the world, you smell the world. Those are avenues of encountering what you don't understand, you can sample them. Your motivations and your emotions provide you with the basic structures of understanding that help you categorize the world. And they're there to begin with. for example, if you say to your wife, "I'm hungry," she doesn't say, "What do you mean, hungry?" And the reason she doesn't say that is because she gets hungry, too. And you can take that for granted. And the reason she gets hungry is because you have a biological system that operates within you. It's a subset of your body that regulates food intake and lets by craving when it is that you need to eat. And that's a universal experience. And it's one way that we parse the world apart instinctively. And if you're hungry, your goal is to find something to eat. And what happens when you're hungry, it isn't a drive that propels you deterministically through the world. What happens when you're hungry is that your hunger takes a grip of your vision, your internal vision. It says, "Your goal is now to find something to eat." And now you're set up in a perceptual frame that orients the world in its entirety around the task that you're undertaking, which is to find food. And the best way to think about hunger is as a personality or as a story. Hunger is the personality or the story that drives you into the realm of conceptualization that has food at its end. In the Exodus story, the Promised Land is the land of milk and honey. And that's partly because archaic people were hungry a lot, and milk is fat and honey is sugar. And when you don't have enough to eat, ice cream, that's sugar and fat, that's paradise. Right. And when you're hungry, food is paradise. And it sets up—it's not a drive. It's not a deterministic drive, because if you're hungry, you might have to solve extremely complex problems, like how to share food with other people, for example, in order to eat. the hunger is a sophisticated subpersonality. And we have a variety of intrinsic, instinctual subpersonalities that we define as motivations that we all share. That's part of what makes us mutually comprehensible and fundamentally human. And various physiologists have broken these motivational states down in various ways. But one reasonable rubric based on biological analysis is that you have two broad classes of motivation. One is designed to make sure that you continue to exist. Those are self-preservation motivations or self-maintenance, and the others are reproductive. And there's you, and you have to keep yourself going, but there's you in the social world, right? you need a mate, and you to get along with other people. And there are different classes of motivation that serve those different needs. in terms of self-maintenance, you get hot or you get cold. If you're taking care of an infant, you see this very clearly, because if your infant is distressed, it's usually because there's some basic motivational need that's not addressed. They're hot, they're cold, they're wet, they're thirsty, they're hungry, they're tired, right? Or they need to use the washroom. It's something like that. And if you're taking care of an infant, you run through these different—is the baby too hot? Is the baby too cold? Does the baby need something to eat? Is the baby tired? And those are your basic initial solutions, and they suffice 95% of the time. And that's a good thing to know, if you have an infant. It's like, you go through the checklist. Even with little kids, it's the same thing. If they start to misbehave, they're often hungry—adults for that matter, too. I noticed when we had little kids that we'd take them out to a social event, and after like an hour, they'd start to misbehave, and then we'd leave, and my wife and I would think, "It was time to go." And the kids figured that out before we did. It's like, the adults will get crabby 15 minutes after the kids get crabby. anyways, you have these basic in-built motivations, and they're there at the beginning. And a two-year-old, for example, is really nothing but a bundle of those motivations. And one of the things that makes kids delightful is they just bounce through those motivational states, and they appear. If a kid's angry, some kids in particular, they'll have a tantrum. It's like, they're just 100% rage. I've seen 30-year-olds have tantrums. I tell you, man, you want to call the police when that happens. It's really terrifying because a two-year-old who's having a tantrum is completely out of control. But they're, like, two. what are they going to do? They're only this tall and you can just push them over if they cause too much trouble. But if you're 30 and you have a tantrum, oh my god, it's quite the terrifying display. And a two-year-old will cry and be enraged and be hungry and then be happy that you can hardly even stand it. Neither can they. And they just cycle through these motivational states. And there's a real purity in that and a real intensity that makes being around them fun. But they can't take care of themselves, and they're nothing but a handful of problems. And if you have someone who's adult who's like that, like, god help you. it's just fine when you're two, but when you're 30, it's getting a little old. One of the things that happens as a child matures, they have these in-built instinctive systems, and maybe that's good enough. And it's not, because the systems really present problems, but they're not that good at offering solutions. when you're hungry, that's not the same as eating. It's the problem. The eating is the solution. The hunger is the problem. When you're thirsty, it's the same thing. These in-built motivational systems don't tell you how to solve the problem. And sometimes the problem is that the motivations conflict. You see this sometimes. Like, are you too hungry to sleep or too tired to eat? And you can see that you can have motivational problems of your own. Maybe you hate someone, but you're terribly sexually attracted to them. that's another place where motivational systems will conflict. And what happens as you mature is that those motivational systems have to be integrated that they can be satisfied over a long period of time, they can be satisfied in relationship to each other, and they can be satisfied in the presence of other people. maybe, you can see that with kids. what are the elementary forms of socialization? Toilet training, because now there are lots of kids who are in grade 1 who aren't toilet-trained. That's become a real problem in places like the UK, is that we've allowed our families to get fragmented that there are six-year-old kids who haven't been toilet-trained. Stunning. And you can see that if you haven't got that figured out by the time you're four, and that's really pushing it, that's going to cause a lot of social problems, to say the least. You're just not getting anywhere in life if you haven't got that under control. And you see that that's a place where a basic biological motivation has to be integrated into a pattern of behavior that's socially acceptable, that other things that are socially acceptable, other solutions that are socially acceptable, can be implemented. And that's what you're trying to do with your children. This is a good thing to know because the Freudian model, which is interesting but wrong, is the human being—it is, but interestingly wrong is useful, right? And it is interestingly wrong. Freud conceptualized us in part as an id, which was a, what would you call, gathering place of instincts, mostly sexual for Freud, but instinct, instinctual compulsion and drive. And that would meet the superego, which was basically the social, patriarchal social community, potentially internalized, that says no. It's inhibition. It's like a Rousseauian model, in some sense, with a bit more negativity added. You're a mass of impulses. The impulses have to be met with control. but that brings us to the force problem. It's like, is it control that you're trying to institute on your children? The problem with that is, if you use force and control, they're going to rebel, or you're going to intimidate them, or you're going to, or you're going to, what would you call? You're going to make them into resentful followers of stupid rules they don't understand, which is also not a good outcome. You can do that to yourself, too, by forcing yourself to do things that you're actually not inclined to do. It's complicated because you want to discipline yourself. what are you doing? you're offering the child a better game. As I said before, my son, when he was little, he was a pretty aggressive little kid. He had a good temper, and I liked playing with him. But now and then he'd get out of hand and get stubborn, and I'd go have him sit on the steps. And it was interesting watching him, because, maybe, it probably happened from the time he was about 12 months till he was about two, something like that. He'd sit on the steps because he, I don't know, he was enraged about something that didn't go his way. And the rule was, sit on the steps until you can play again, until you can act like a civilized human being that other people would like to have around. And as soon as he would do that, he could get off the steps. It was interesting watching him do that, because he'd sit on the steps with his fists clenched, his teeth clenched, and I'd go tap and say, "Are you ready to get off the steps?" "Not yet." But you could see, what was happening is, he was trying to integrate those powerful forces of rage into a personality that would enable him to maintain his social relations. Now, look. If you can imagine this as an adult, is maybe you're having a difficult conversation with your wife, and she's afraid to do that because you have a temper, which means that you're not socialized. She'll say something provocative, maybe that's just related to an actual problem, or maybe she's given you a poke just to find out what son of a bitch you are, and you can't control your anger. And what does that mean? It means that you haven't mastered the capacity to integrate the full range of your aggression into a sophisticated personality. That makes you dangerous. Part of the reason you see that in a developing relationship, for example, between a man and a woman, both partners will test each other out. And women will say provocative things to men. And men think, "Why the hell is that going on?" And the answer is something like, the women want to find out, if you're annoyed, if you turn into a murderous tyrant, because if you do, you're probably not the best person to have around children. And that's a really crucial thing to discover. And you don't discover that just by asking someone. You have to poke them a bunch and see. It's like, can I elicit something in you that's untoward? And that's a deadly game. And it's not even necessary that the people who are playing it even know they are, but people will definitely play games like that, and they need to because you need to know. And it isn't that you control your temper. There are times when you have to, but that's not right. My son, who learned to integrate the part of him that was aggressive, became a very good athlete, and he's very competitive. He really likes to win, and his mother is like that as . But he learned how to—that meant the aggression is still there, but it's replicated at a higher level of development that integrates it with all sorts of other things. If you want to be aggressive while you're playing a sport, you have to play it in a way that other people want to play with. Then you get to have your aggression, but in these walled boundaries. And partly what you're trying to do with your children is to teach them the sophisticated games that enable all of their needs and wants to be met over the longest possible span of time in the broadest possible set of situations. And that's not inhibition. It's not superego against id. It's the integration of those lower-order personalities into a higher-order personality that does meet all the demands. And maybe by the time you're 13 or 14, 15, you're sophisticated enough as a male that you can do a good job playing competitively on a sports team, and you're a good team player, and you give credit where credit is due, and you don't take all the glory when you win, and people like you, and you're a winner, and that makes you attractive. And now your self-maintenance goals and the integration of your personality has also made you sexually and socially attractive, right? And then you're playing a very complex and sophisticated game that meets all of the requirements of those subordinate systems simultaneously, and even more importantly, does that in a way that enables other people to do it at the same time, and maybe even better than they could if you weren't around. Right, and when you think your personality, you might think your personality has a goal. That's an interesting way of thinking about it. You can see what your goal is, the intrinsic goal of your personality, by asking yourself to imagine what it is that you might want. This is a very good exercise. We'll talk about this tomorrow, practically speaking. But you could imagine, daydream, . If your life could be set up the way that you wanted it to, we're assuming you bring a bit of wisdom to bear on this. what would that look like? Probably you'd want to have a partner, and maybe you'd want her to like you, and maybe you'd like to have a family, and the same thing would apply there. You could get along with your parents. You could get along with your siblings. You love your children, and they would respect you. You'd have some friends. if you could have the friends you wanted, what would that look like? And what would your friendships be like? You could do that with your career, and you can do that with your education. We'll step through this tomorrow when we talk about these things more concretely. But those are all those visions of what you want and need, if you're asking yourself honestly, are the collective voice of your integrated instincts that are attempting to lay out a description of who you could be if you could satisfy everything that needs to be satisfied at the same time. Now, you imagine it's three in the morning and you've done something stupid and your conscience comes to visit; and it's bothering you because you are a fool and it. what the hell is that voice of conscience? Is it you? And if it's you, why can't you just shut it off? And if it's you, why is it calling you to task? Why can't you just tell your conscience, "Reorient yourself there, buddy. I can do whatever the hell I want. I don't want to feel guilty about it afterwards. I don't want to feel disgusted or ashamed or that I'm lesser. Why would I bother with that?"
