Now, you can tell your kids, "Don't sell your soul that you're a member of the group." That's a whole different discussion because you don't want to pretend that you're something that you're not. You don't want to sacrifice the possibility of your higher-order being to idiot identification with the whim of the crowd. But that's not the same thing as, "It shouldn't matter to you what your friends think." what person it doesn't matter to what other people think? That's a psychopath. And most of the time, you should be damn concerned with what other people think. Not always, and that's a tight discrimination. But most of the time, if most people think there's something wrong with you, they're probably right. Sometimes they're not. And that's an edge case. All right. Another way of looking at emotions. You move from the present to the future. There are things that you predict that are going the way you want them to. That fills you with positive emotion. And then there's a category of obstacle—we'll talk about this tomorrow—there's a category of obstacle that's unpredictable. Sometimes you'll run into obstacles that how to move, and sometimes you'll run into obstacles whose nature you don't understand and you can't predict. You run into something you don't understand about your husband, for example. It's a bottomless mystery, and we'll talk about that a little bit tomorrow. three categories of stimuli that you respond to emotionally. Things that get you on your way, things that get in your way, and things you don't understand. And the things you don't understand, that's a bottomless pit. That's a hole. We'll talk about that tomorrow. I'll close with this one today. I showed you one of these little story frames, right? You're here. That's the present. You're aiming at something. The world orients itself that there are pathways forward to that. You want the pathway because otherwise your plan is invalidated or you'll be upset. You don't want too many obstacles. You want things to help you along your way. That's the world. You're always in a little frame like that. those frames are nested, and that nesting is your identity. When you're developing a vision, you're developing the entire nested structure. I'll show you how that works. your identity is not something you carry around in your head. now you're two and you have all these motivational forces working within you. as you mature, you integrate them, and you integrate them in a way that makes you a good player within the family and then within your friends. you integrate those instincts in an increasingly social environment. And then as you mature more, you get better and better at doing that, across longer and longer spans of time, in more and more situations with more and more people. let's break that down. This will show you how you move from the abstract moral imperative to the particular. you tell your child to make dinner, and he's three. he looks at you. "What do you mean?" And you give him a cuff because he's too stupid to make dinner. This is not a good plan. And what's your problem? The problem is he's three. why is that a problem? And the problem is he doesn't know what complete, make dinner means. He doesn't know the micro steps. When you say to someone, "Make dinner," you're assuming that they know how to make dinner. You're assuming that they've been socialized the same way you have been, that when you utter that phrase, they understand what it means. we decompose that. What does it mean to make dinner? my son's 15 months old, and he's starting to learn to set the table. But you can't say "set the table," partly because he can't even see the table. It's here and he's this high. But you can say, "Do where the knife drawer is?" He'll go, "Yes." Say, "Go to the knife drawer." He goes to the knife drawer. "Pull the knife drawer open. Feel around till you feel a knife." He'll do that. You can give him a pat on the head. "Good work. Got the knife?" "Yes." "Take the knife into the table and put it on the top of the table." what has he done? He's started to set the table. You see, you've broken it down, right? And you've broken it down to implementable subroutines. setting the table is an integrated story. It's part of an identity. It's an integrated story that involves a variety of mastered subroutines. Part of what you're doing when you're learning a new task is you have to break the task down to the level of subroutine that you need to master. Right, and when you're training someone, the first thing you have to find out is, what don't they know? Maybe you're training someone for customer service. It's like, maybe they whisper on the phone. You might want to find that out. Do how to talk? You might assume yes, and that assumption might be completely wrong. Maybe they have to triple the volume of their voice. You have to play until you find out at what level of the subroutines the person is lacking. That includes you, and you build it from the bottom up. it's cut vegetables, set table, do dishes. that's part of completing a meal. Now, if you're a halfway civilized five-year-old, maybe you can make a basic meal. then you can say to your five-year-old, "how to make some Kraft dinner?" And they've got that. They know where the pots are, they know how to boil water. you can now tag that whole complex small subpersonality with a single verbal tag, and they can do it. maybe if you're a good father, how to make a meal, how to play with the baby. And what do you do when you play with the baby? you play peekaboo, you tickle the baby, you clean the baby. Those are subroutines. Now how to take care of the baby, and how to make a meal. And maybe that's part of being a good parent. And that's part of what makes you a good partner. And that's part of what makes you a good person. And you can say to your wife, "Be a good person." It's like, maybe you tell your kids that, "Be good." And sometimes they know what you mean, but you probably have to decompose that down the hierarchy of identity till you hit the level at which they're insufficient and repair that. Imagine you're playing the piano, playing a complex melody, and you trip over a note, and you do that repeatedly. what you do is, you slow down, and then you concentrate on the place where you made a mistake, and then you see what you're doing when you make the mistake, and then you adjust that, and then you practice the adjustment till you've automated it, then you integrate it in the rhythm, then you play the whole phrase, and then you go over it. That's exactly what you do when you're trying to solve a problem of adaptation. You hit an obstacle, you decompose it down the hierarchy of specialization till you see where the error is, the minimal error, rectify that, practice the rectification, and then sequence back up. And then you're aiming always up. When you're training your two-year-old to put a butter knife on the table, it's a subset of helping him become a good person. But that good person isn't some disembodied abstraction. It's the integrated hierarchy of a set of leveled specializations all aiming in the same direction. I'll close with this. Here's a way of conceptualizing that. you have a highly skilled athlete on your team who's also elected by his peers to be the captain of the team because of his leadership abilities. then you can imagine what athlete means in that context. It means, possibly, he's the most skilled player on the team. But what do you mean skilled? maybe he can score the most goals, but that's not sufficient, right? He needs to score the most goals in a way that motivates everyone else on the team to score the most goals themselves and to improve in their capacity to do that over time and not to be jealous of the differences in skill at the team level and to get along in a way that makes the entire enterprise worth replicating over and over. And if you do that, then you're a skilled athlete. And that's the same in the broader moral domain, is you want to be skilled at the specific things that you do. You want to have the perceptions and the actions at hand that enable you to do that. But you want to have them integrated into a personality that makes all of the games that you're playing work in a broader game and work repetitively with other people in a self-improving direction. If you do that, your life will be meaningful, because meaning is the instinct that tells you that you're doing that. It's not some metaphysical abstraction that you can eradicate with, like, a nihilistic rationalism. "What's the point of life?" It's an experiential reality. It means that you're existing in harmony with your integration towards the highest possible purpose. That's a good way of thinking about. Your conscience will aid you in that, and will the manifestation of your interests. tomorrow, we'll talk about how to make that concrete, to bring it all the way down to Earth, because you can do that. You can and you need to. All right. Thank you very much.

title: Plan - 4. Fear as a Catalyst
content: All right, I titled this course Vision and Plan: Theory and Practice, and made the case, at least implicitly, yesterday, that the way that you structure your life has multiple levels of resolution, in the higher order and more abstract levels, like ethical principles and high-order visions. And then that has to be scaled down to where it touches the ground, to speak, which is where you can make implementable changes. And they're usually small, but those small changes, even though they might be troublesome, even those small changes are still necessarily related to the structure of the whole. That's actually what gives them their meaning. If you're doing -called small things. And one of the things that's useful to know, too, is that if you understand the relationship between the part and the whole, which isn't much different than understanding the relationship between you and the world, then that can also imbue all the things that you do at a micro level with meaning, which is what you want. Because you want things in your life to be worth the trouble, . yesterday, I gave you some background theory, and that's useful. A lower resolution theory, one that's more abstract, has the advantage of covering more situations and the disadvantage of less specificity. And today we're going to try to make things specific, but tie them back to the more abstract higher-order principles that we discussed yesterday. today we're going to talk about practice, vision and plan, theory and practice. Yesterday we talked about vision and theory, and today we'll talk about plan and practice. I read this interesting animal study years ago, when I was first investigating the neuropsychology and neurophysiology of motivation and emotion. I read a lot of animal experimental studies. And from the 1940s till about the 1990s, a lot of psychology concentrated on animal behavior, laboratory studies of laboratory animals. And the people who did those studies, Skinner was the person who first really zeroed in on this; they were very, very careful thinkers. The behaviorists were narrow, partly because they were dealing with micro elements of behavior. But man, I tell you, as far as precision of thought goes, those people had it. They had it locked down. And Skinner, for example, was extremely good at detailing out theories of learning, theories of reinforcement, emotion, motivation, reward, punishment, threat, etc. And out of his work, I would say, the whole domain of neuroscience emerged. And one of the mediating people in that process was Jeffrey Gray, who wrote a book in 1982 called the Neuropsychology of Anxiety, which is an absolutely superb book looking at the relationship between emotional response and brain function—brain function anatomically and also pharmacologically. That's useful because if you can see something that works behaviorally, anatomically, and pharmacologically, and you get the same results, in relationship to your theory, using all three different methods of approach, you can be pretty sure that you're onto something real. And I don't think there was a book published in the last half of the 20th century that was a more profound psychological work than The Neuropsychology of Anxiety. Gray, who was quite the genius, was a student of Hans Eysenck, who was the most published psychologist of the last half of the 20th century, who was also a very careful thinker. Gray detailed out a lot of animal behavioral studies. I don't know how many citations he had in his book. Like, 1800? Something insane. 1800, scientific papers. That's the equivalent of 600 PhD dissertations. that's how much work he did to write that book. Seems almost incalculable, but yeah, yeah, yeah. One of the studies he detailed, which was extremely interesting, had to do with animal motivation. And it's a good example of how you can find out very important things by looking at micro details. You can tell how motivated a rat is to do something by how hard it will work to get access to the opportunity to do it. It's like how you can tell how much you want something, too. If you want something. What do you mean "want", exactly? You say you want it; does that mean you want it? These things are very—people throw around these words like, "I feel like I need this." None of that makes any sense. That utterance has virtually no meaning. What do you mean by that? Do you really want something? What are you willing—how do we know if you want it? How about, what are you willing to give up for it? What are you willing to invest in it? What are you willing to sacrifice for it? How much work are you willing to do for it? one of the things they used to do with rats is, you can tell how hungry a rat is. Maybe you deprive it of food. Skinner deprived his rats of food till they were down to 75% of their normal body weight. they're actually pretty hungry. How could you tell how hungry they were? one of the things you could do is, if you trained a rat, for example, to run down a little runway to get a food reward, you could tie a spring scale to its tail and see how hard it would pull and for how long. And then you have a behavioral measurement of something like motivation. And if you feed a rat a lot and you put it in a situation where it can run down a runway and get access to food, but it's satiated, it's not going to pull at all. And you think, this behaviorist would have said, "You don't even need the word want in a situation like that. You don't need to infer any internal states." Now, they went a little bit too far with that presupposition, but they could actually measure it. It's like, hungry, "hungry" rat will pull hard against a obstacle to get access to food. It's like a definition of want. Definition of whether or not you want something might not be how much squawking you're willing to do if you don't get it, but how much work you're willing to put in to increase the probability that it'll happen. And that's a sacrificial assessment. And we have a sacrificial relationship with the world. That's a good way of thinking about. It's quite strange that human beings do this, because one of the things we presume axiomatically is that if we're willing to give up certain things in the present, that we can gain some reward in the future. That's what you do when you work. It's like the definition of work. One of the mysteries of the Old Testament, for example, is that there's an insistence in the stories that human beings live in a sacrificial relationship to what's divine. That's why there's much emphasis on sacrifice in the biblical writings. And it's not easy to exactly make sense of that because it's couched in an archaic language. But the fundamental assumption is, you make a deal with reality. You live in a contractual relationship with the future. And the presumption is that, if you put in your time and effort now—and that's what work is, because maybe work is something you wouldn't do intrinsically for the reward of the moment, unless you're very fortunate in your work. You give something up, your time, your energy, other opportunities, because you feel if you make the investment, then the payoff will be worth it. And that's a contractual relationship with other people. But in some really abstract sense, with the future itself, or even with the structure of existence itself, it's like, you strike a bargain and you're supposed to hold up your end of the bargain. And we presume that if we do hold up our end of the bargain that things will turn out the way we would like them to turn out. And that's a strange thing, that can actually work. And it's also something that really is quite peculiar to human beings because most animals have a very short-term orientation to gratification. Short-term and narrowly self-centered. A grizzly bear is out for himself. Now there's a certain amount of planning, but most of that's just running on instinct. Whereas you can conceive of an abstract formulation of the future and do all sorts of strange things in the present to strike the bargain that might make that come about. And that's very strange that people do that. And we do do that. And, back to motivation, with the rats. How do how motivated a rat is? How hard will it pull against an obstacle to obtain a goal? And that's a measure of how hungry a rat might be. A rat will work for a reward. there's another thing you could do, is maybe the rat is running towards some food at the end of a laboratory setup, and you can measure how fast the rat runs. And then you could assume that the faster the rat runs, the more motivated he is to get to the end. a hungry rat will run pretty fast down the runway to get to the reward. But here's something else that's interesting about rats, is they don't like cats at all, not even a bit. And they dislike cats much that rats that have never encountered a cat can be thrown into an absolute rat frenzy by the odor of a cat. there is—rats are as unhappy about cats as we are about snakes, or maybe more. And a rat's—if you waft in cat odor into a rat cage, the rats will get the hell away from the cat odor. And rats are very, very good at odor detection, partly because we've been trying to poison them for, like, 50,000 years, right? In fact, I read that if a rat eats something and gets sick, and the other rats know it, and the rats have smelled the breath of the rat that got sick, they won't eat whatever it was the rat ate. that's pretty sensitive. And anyways, rats don't like cat odor. And imagine now you have a rat that's hungry and it's going to run down the runway to get to the food at some rate, but then you waft in some cat odor behind it. And now the rat's running away from the cat and towards the food. Then it's really moving. you could imagine if you were running a race as an athlete that you'd be cruising along at a pretty good rate because you want to win, because that's the reward. But then maybe they release a grizzly bear behind you, and then you find a little bit more motivation. And that's worth knowing because the—see, the lesson you can derive from that is that it's something to be motivated by reward. And that's the most desirable form of motivation. now when a rat is running down a runway and it's hungry and it's running towards the food, it's going to go eat the food, and that'll satiate it. And then it won't be hungry and that motivational frame will disappear. And it's happy when it's running down the runway because it can see that it's moving towards the reward. And as I described yesterday, that's the basis for incentive reward. That's the basis for enthusiasm. It's, it's the meaning that characterizes hope and curiosity and forward, forward motion, voluntary forward motion. That's all tied up with positive emotion that's mediated by a system, the dopaminergic system. Neurochemically, that's the same system, that cocaine activates. And most drugs that people take for fun, that they abuse, directly activate the system that makes you think you're doing something worthwhile when you're moving towards a goal. that's very interesting to know as . And that can motivate you quite a lot. But if you're terrified and something's chasing you and you're moving towards something you value, then you really might be something to contend with. And you can build that into your vision. And that's a good thing to do. this—these little diagrams here are quite interesting. the one on the left is a vision of heaven, and the one on the right is a vision of Dante's hell. And you see, they're multilayered like that. Remember that diagram I showed you yesterday, where we moved up from the very specifics of setting the table to the very abstract, being a good person. It's a hierarchy of identity. there's a heavenly hierarchy of identity, and that's the identity that would be you, as you're moving towards all the good things you could be and have, at all the levels that would have to be implemented. And then there's a hellish hierarchy, which is where you could end up if you did all the stupid things that you could imagine doing very badly. And maybe to be optimally, optimally motivated, you need a vision of exactly how bad things could turn out for you if you manage to make all the wrong choices, and a vision of just how good things could be if you had enough sense to walk uphill. And you might think, "I don't need to contemplate the negative." But then I would say, "maybe you don't want to forego the utility of having your negative emotions push you along, because they're very powerful motivating forces." And one of the things I certainly saw as a clinician was that it's better to have your fear behind you, pushing you forward, than your fear in front of you, stopping you. I can give you a concrete example of that. imagine that you're in a job that you hate, or a marriage you hate, or something you hate, and you're afraid to confront it. And your fear's in front of you, manifesting itself as an obstacle. And you can understand why you might be afraid to confront it, because imagine that you've been laboring in a job for 10 years. It's a miserable, wretched occupation. You hate virtually everything about it. And now you turn around, you decide to confront it, and now you have to go down the levels of analysis to find out why you were bloody stupid that you wasted a whole decade of your precious life doing something absolutely, unbearably miserable for no reason at all. When you get to the bottom of that, you find out that, in some fundamental way, you betrayed yourself. That's not much fun, especially because you're not going to get that decade back. And often what people do, although it's not that clear—sometimes if you've done something spectacularly stupid and you delve into it and you fix it, you can derive all the wisdom you could have accrued over that decade from that investigation. And then you can turn the negative thing you did into something positive. But that's not an easy thing to do. That's a confession and a redemption and an atonement. But you have to go through the painful process, which really means that you have to face all the things that you were avoiding during that entire 10-year period. Now you can do that, and that's one of the ways you can set your life right. But you can certainly understand why people don't want to do that because it's quite the trip down Dante's Inferno right to the bottom. And "Why bother?" And the answer is, do you want to spend the next 20 years doing the same thing. it's like you're picking your hell. You can pick one that you could walk through voluntarily and repair, or you could just pick one that you'll just stay in for the rest of your miserable life. And if you're properly afraid of that latter option, then maybe you can put your fear behind you and that'll be one of the things that'll motivate you to confront what's stopping you. when I would talk to my clients, for example, and they were afraid to switch jobs, one of the things we would do is, fine, don't switch jobs. All right, now, let's play a little game. "How angry, resentful, bitter, arrogant, and deceitful are you at the moment, because of your job and the misery that is encompassing you because of your job?" then, you can walk someone through that, let them talk about that, really explore it. Then you can say, "you've been in this miserable job for 10 years. Has that made you better or worse?" And the answer usually is "worse." "Stronger or weaker?" "Weaker." "Has it damaged your relationship with your family and the world?" And the answer to that's usually yes. And you've got older, 10 years, it's like, now it's 15 years in the future and you haven't done a damn thing to fix that. All right, now, what are you like? you're 15 years older, you're 15 years smaller. You're less healthy, you're less prepared psychologically. You're less likely to fix it then than you would now because there's less of you. You wait for a bus for half an hour; it's supposed to be there for five minutes. You don't want to leave because you already wasted half an hour waiting. you wait another two hours. You should cut your losses. But people don't do that. You think you're going to cut your losses when it's 20 years that you've done the same stupid thing instead of 10? No. And all that's happening as you prolong your agony is that you get smaller and the agony gets greater. And then you have to think about exactly what person you're going to be like in 10 years if you allow that to happen. And then—think about it, I don't mean just some abstract semantic representation that's bloodless. I mean to bloody think about it. Envision it, imagine it, daydream about it. You don't have that much life, and you've let it go. Now you're older and you're bitter and you're not much fun to be around, and most of the joy's gone out of your life. And maybe you're like, I've seen people. They hit 50, they've had a lot of things pile up around them. They haven't cleaned up the mess, and now they're 50 and they don't have that much time left, not much youthful time, and they didn't have the bloody energy to clean up the mess in the last 20 years. What's the probability that they're going to start now? And sometimes they can turn things around and, as I said, you can break things down into small pieces and start moving ahead. And maybe there's no point in your life where the situation is absolutely hopeless. But, man. I had a great conversation with an artist friend of mine once, and he said, "you see people who—the mess around them is large that there's not enough energy left in them to fix it." then you're done, right? Because barring a miracle, and you maybe don't want to discount that possibility, you're just not going to manage it. And I've had people like that now and then in my clinical practice, where no matter how much digging we did, there was much to be dug up that it would have taken three lifetimes to fix. And then, what do you do? Yeah, you throw up your hands and probably you leave because there's nothing you can do. All right, we, with my colleagues, Daniel Higgins and Robert Pihl—Pihl was my graduate supervisor at McGill, Higgins, a student of mine at Harvard—and I've worked with these two men for 30 years now, with Bob for even longer than that, had a great relationship with him as a supervisor. Daniel was a wonderful student of mine and has been a very good business collaborator. We tried to make some of this practical. And 30 years ago, we decided we were going to put this company together that would produce psychological interventions. We had a bunch of rules for that. They had to be low-cost; free, is not a good price. People ask me sometimes online why I haven't made these intervention available for free. And the first answer to that is, what do you mean free? Someone's paying for it, and the logical person to pay for something that the person is using is the person that's using it, not the person that's providing it. And one of our rules right at the beginning of our enterprise was that we weren't going to produce micro businesses that weren't self-sustaining. Another reason for that is if your endeavor can't stand on its own two feet, what the hell makes you think it's worth pursuing? One of the advantages to being embedded in a market environment is you get signals. If I'm trying to produce a psychological intervention, and no one wants it, then I've probably designed it badly or marketed it badly, or I'm trying to solve a problem that's not actually a problem, or my solution isn't a good one. And if you put a reasonable price on something, the reasonable price would be one that enables the project to sustain itself and possibly grow. Which is why you need profit, which is often regarded as a dirty word. It's like, you work for profit. If you're not working for profit, all you ever do is work because the work is just enough that you can continue the work. why would you work then? Just to not die? And fair enough, but that's a hell of a harsh motivation. Do this or I'll shoot you. That's not a great way of motivating yourself optimally. you want to set up an enterprise that generates a profit that you have something to play with. It's not you can go gratify all your idiot hedonistic whims. And maybe you can get away with that for a while and spend all your ill-gotten capitalist gain on hookers and cocaine. But it's not a very good long-term strategy. If you have any sense, you take what you've earned in profit, you reinvest it either in the company it can keep growing and you can provide more services, maybe at a lower cost, or maybe you can go do something else somewhat creative and useful with the surplus. That's what you should be doing. And people who are radically successful at continued entrepreneurial ventures, that's really what they do. If you're a mafioso boss, and all you're interested in is power and luxury, first of all, that's a movie. It's not something that's going to work in your life. And even if you do try to implement that, it will probably only work for about 10 years before you're either dead of your own stupidity or someone will do you the favor of putting you out of your misery. This is not a good plan. And then you think, how much should you charge for a product? And the answer is, this is the answer—what the market will bear. Because imagine that I put together a program that, if you did, wouldn't take very long and would change your life and positively and maybe permanently. what's that worth? in the Soviet Union, they had a central pricing committee. They had to make something like 10,000 pricing decisions a day. if you ever start a company, the first thing you're—one of the first things you're going to find out is, it's really hard to figure out what your damn product is worth. I mean, maybe I make a program that'll help you make a vision. I charge you $10,000 for it. Now, why? maybe if you paid $10,000, you'd take it seriously, and maybe you'd be happy to pay $10,000 because you want to indicate to yourself that you've made a sacrifice that indicates that you think that putting that much time into yourself is worthwhile. And maybe instead it's 50 cents. It's like, if it's 50 cents, everyone could do it, but then it's 50 cents. And if there's something online for 50 cents, what's the probability that you're going to think it's worth anything? And you might think it should be free. It's like, we already discussed the problems with free, but how much should you pay? here's another problem is, most people want to trade. They don't want charity, and if you offer people the opportunity to engage in an enterprise that you've established, they would like to repay the favor that they keep the slate clean. Because most people are sensible enough to know that you shouldn't be accruing unreturned favors as you move through life. And you also want to put the price at something that's fair. the person can think, "The provider of the service did their part in providing the service, but I did my part in paying for the service." And part of the way that societies stay productive, generous, and abundant is that deal, that mutual deal, is made honestly and voluntarily. you can go into a store and buy a piece of clothing and you don't have to feel like you did anyone a favor or vice versa. It's just an even trade. And it sums to zero or maybe to mutual benefit, which is actually the case. And you can just do that repeatedly. And that's the utility of setting up a system where the trade is voluntary. And then people will participate in it on a voluntary basis too. It's not based on force or charity or pity or any of those things that sometimes sound good, but you have hidden prices. anyways, the other rule that we put into place was that, while we wanted psychological interventions that were of demonstrable utility, we had to demonstrate to ourselves and generally by publishing that the intervention worked, it had to be profitable. But as reasonable a cost as we could manage, because we wanted to offer it to as many people as possible. It had to be scalable, if the enterprise grew—if your enterprise isn't designed properly and starts to scale, it can collapse under its own weight. you have to think about what you would do if you became successful, how you would scale upwards. we wanted it to have minimal bureaucratic understructure. And we've run this company for 30 years, literally with, we have three people and one part-time person who handles customer service. And we're able to, what would you say? We've offered our products to 150,000 people, something like that, with no infrastructure whatsoever. we've been able to keep the price down there, too. Now we have built this program called Self-Authoring that helps people write an autobiography. It helps them evaluate their faults and their virtues in the present and then it helps them develop a vision for the future. And it corresponds in some ways to the map I showed you yesterday of past, present, and future. And the idea is you want to iron out all the kinks in your life. maybe you have to iron out your past a bit because you're carrying some baggage along with you. And maybe you need to figure out what your virtues are and your talents in the present and what your faults are, you can capitalize on your virtues and talents and rectify your faults. Then maybe you need to lay out a vision for the future. And there's a big literature on such things, from two sources. One, the clinical psychological domain, showing that if you get people to write about past traumatic events voluntarily, that increases their physical and mental health. And another that shows if you get them to write about their future, that does the same thing. And then a literature from the management side of psychology, psychology of business, that if you have employees and you want to motivate them— Imagine that if I wanted to motivate you, I could ask you to lay out a plan about how you were going to be a good employee for the next year or five years into the future. Seems like a reasonable thing to do. But man, imagine you could match that against another experimental group where, instead of writing about how you were going to be a productive and generous employee, you wrote about what you were going to do with your life and how your job might fit into that. what you find is that if you get people to do the latter instead of the former, that the effects are much more positive. And you could imagine that the reason for that is, is that if I hire you, one of the things I'm going to want to know is, why is working for me or with me, which is a better way of thinking about it, what is that going to do for you? You're going to want to tell me what it's going to do for me, because that's, at least in principle, part of the reason I might hire you. If you're in a job interview, you might want to tell the person why you're going to be useful to them. But this is a more subtle thing to contemplate, is one of the things you want to tell them is why it would be useful for you to be working here. And the reason for that is, if you're making a partnership with someone, which is really what you're doing even if you hire them, if you have any sense, is you want to know why. I would like to set up a situation where, if I just ignore you, if I have to, you'll go out and work like a mad dog without me having a micromanage or supervise you. And then I can be certain you're going to do that, if I know that our interests are aligned in relationship to your own goals. I want to know that if you come to work for me, that you have a reason for that. Which also implies that you have a reason. And you get your employees, for example, to lay out a vision for their life, and then if they find out too, that it turns out that the job they have isn't in keeping with the vision for their life that they want to pursue, then really it's like, "Sayonora, man. Nice working with you. You should go find a place that suits what you're aiming at because it'd be better for you and be better for me. There's just no reason for us to be partnering," which is what you do if you're an employee and you have any sense. There's no reason for us to be partnering unless your needs and wants, the genuine ones, are met by our contractual arrangement. See, and this is a good thing to know if you're a manager, because you don't want to be imposing a motivational framework on someone. You'll have to use power to control them then. And part of the problem with that, maybe you want power because you're completely out of your bloody mind, but what power really means is, I have to stand over you with a stick, unless I'm a bit on the sadistic side and I'm looking for an opportunity to whack you for idiot reasons of my own. I'd much rather know that you're doing these things for your own purposes. I'd like to know what those purposes are, and I'd hope that they would run in alignment with mine. That's what happens when you play a game with someone, and it's a voluntary game. And you see this with children when they, once they're three or and they can start engaging in pretend games. What they do when they set up a pretend play opportunity, say, they want to play houses, they invite the other child to play. "Do you want to play house? Do you want to play tag? Do you want to play hide-and-go-seek?" And part of the rule is the other person has to want to play. And then you see, you can enter into the same shared frame of reference. Your emotions line up, and do your motivations. And then you can walk in lockstep towards the hypothetical goal. that's a very good deal. And it's a good deal to do that with yourself, too, that you're not standing over yourself with a stick, beating yourself that you move forward. Maybe that's better than being completely useless and laying in your bed being nihilistic and depressed. But it's not an optimal solution. You want to entice yourself forward to the degree that that's possible, and you want to get your fears in order. when we built this future authoring program, one of the things we did was try to operationalize this, to bring these abstractions down to earth. ? here's what you do at the beginning of this exercise. And you don't need to purchase the program to do this, you can just do it yourself. But the program makes it easier because it's all laid out. But I'll walk through it. Now what we found, we used this program in three separate research studies. At McGill University, which is a selective state school, that's a good way of thinking about it. I'd say it's probably a 90th-percentile-tier university by American standards. It would be less elite than the Ivy leagues in the U.S., but it would be the next tier. that's what McGill is. And we ran it at the business school in Rotterdam and at a community college/trade school in Ontario. we hit a variety of different academic domains. And what we did is, we had students come in and they would either do this vision program for 90 minutes or they would write about—they would write an equivalent amount about what they'd done in the last two weeks. We're just controlling for the fact of a psychological intervention and the fact of writing. And we found that, at McGill, students who did the program, their grades went up 35% and their dropout rate plummeted. These were students who are already in school. I think, on average, they were second- or third-year students. At Mohawk College, we had students do it before they enrolled in there, when they were going to be familiarized with the university, before attending in the summer. They did it for 90 minutes with no preparation. They got no feedback for their writing. We dropped their dropout rate by 50% with a 90-minute intervention. And the biggest effects, and this was true in the study at Rotterdam too, the biggest effects actually occurred with the students who had the worst academic background and who were the least likely to perform at university by, if you used their race and their ethnicity and their sex to predict their probability of continuing. it actually did the most, it had the most effect for the least promising students, which was fascinating because, most of the time, it's one of the terrible things about psychological interventions. Imagine you have a group of kids who are performing from bad to good, and you put in an intervention. Often, what happens is the students who are doing do even better. It has hardly any effect at all on the poor performers. It's part of that Matthew principle I talked about earlier, that if you already have, you'll get more, and if you don't have, it'll be taken away from you. It's very hard to come up with an intervention that actually lifts up the bottom end, regardless of how positive you are about your intervention. Another thing you learn as a social scientist, and every politician should know this is, just because you think you have the proper outcome in mind doesn't mean you do have the proper outcome in mind. And it certainly doesn't mean that your stupid intervention is going to do only the good things you think it will do and nothing else. And it's often the case with broad-scale psychological or social interventions that the unintended consequences of the intervention are negative that they just demolish anything positive and are often counterproductive. that's a terrifying thing to understand, the law of unintended consequences. But it's an ethical rule if you're a social—if you're a social scientist, that if you're going to intervene in people's lives, that you build in an assessment of your intervention to ensure that what you're doing actually works, instead of making people worse. A good example of that is the self-esteem movement that the idiots, educational psychologists implemented almost nationwide 20 years ago. All they managed to do was to make kids more neurotic and experience higher levels of negative emotion. And they confused narcissism with self-esteem and taught a generation to also be narcissistic. making children more narcissistic and miserable doesn't count as a success unless part of you is aiming at that, which, and that was a suspicion I couldn't squelch when I saw that form of stupidity being purveyed out into the educational universe. Whole word reading was another cataclysmic example of that. dim-witted psychologists noted that excellent readers maybe read a whole phrase in a glance and certainly a word, they're not sounding out the damn word. And they derived from that the proposition that, if you wanted to teach children to read, you should teach them to identify whole words, instead of noticing that we actually have a phonetic alphabet, which is like a discovery crucial it's like discovering the wheel. And that by teaching children to identify words, whole words, we're trying to make them learn English like Chinese people learn Chinese, which is insane that only someone idiotic and educated could possibly think it up. And the consequence of that—and they implemented in California first—was that reading ability in California plummeted. I think it went from first in the US to 51st over the course of about five years. I don't still think they've shaken that stupidity out of the education system. anyways, you test your damn interventions to see if they work. And maybe you do a micro project first to make sure you're not doing anything cataclysmic before you launch it into the entire population. in any case, students' grades at McGill went up 35%, their dropout rate went down. And we found that the dropout rate at Mohawk College went down by 50%. And then we found similar results at the business school in Rotterdam. And the groups that benefited most there, the stratification for success was, like, Caucasian women were doing the best, then non-Caucasian women, then non-Caucasian, then Caucasian men, then non-Caucasian men. That was the stratification of academic achievement at the business school. Now there were more men than women. the women were a more elite group. And that's part of the reason they were doing better. Although women tend to be doing better academically than men across the board now, all the way from junior high through the entire education system. The biggest effect was on the non-Caucasian men. And in fact, in our Rotterdam group, the intervention had such a big effect that the non-Caucasian men outperformed the Caucasian women as the program moved forward across a couple of years. that was cool. And one of the things we concluded from that, I don't know if it's true, is that, if men are motivated by their own purposes, they will succeed. But if they're only in a system because the system has a structure, they're going to be all over the place. And I think that's probably because men are more disagreeable than women. And unless they're motivated, unless they're self-motivated, they're just not going to participate. And anyways, the consequence of that was that absolutely zero universities picked up the programs, even the ones where we did the bloody studies, even when we worked with the universities where we did the studies for, like, a year afterwards, trying to adjust our technology to their systems, even after they promised us they would implement them, which indicated to us that they could care less whether half their bloody students dropped out, which is a complete catastrophe. There's a school—Larry Arnn runs it—Hillsdale. It's a conservative college in the northeast U.S. They have a 1% dropout rate. you can get there if you run things properly. It's like 50%; it's absolutely inexcusable. And it was quite a mystery too. Took me a long time to think through. We have people sit down and write for 90 minutes about what they would want in their life and who they would want to be. Now this is a pretty fundamental thing to do. You'd think that if you educated children for 15 years, that, at some point, you might take an afternoon to have them sit down and write seriously about their vision for themselves and themselves in relationship to the world. You might think that would be important that it's self-evident and that, maybe for a semester, you might do nothing other than that. Yeah, I learned, because I looked into the history of the development of the education system, that the public education system in the West was predicated on the Prussian military model developed in the mid-1800s. And the purpose of the Prussian military schools was to produce obedient and will-less soldiers. And then that was imported into the US by industrialists who were fascists. And this was before the Second World War, when being a fascist wasn't quite the dismal enterprise that it then became, to train the children of rural people who were flooding into the cities to become obedient workers. Not to become people who could manage their own lives, right, but people who would show up and do things in order by the bell. And there was some utility in that because rural people were flooding into the cities, and industrialization was taking place. And the most likely life outcome for many of those children was that they were going to be working in a factory, and they needed to be socialized in order to do that. But taking away their own autonomy and subjugating their will to the corporate, what would you say, the fascist corporate endeavor, hardly seems to be an optimized solution to that problem, but it's still the one that we implement, literally 130 years later. God, dismal, dismal. Anyways. how do you do this? do I have that quote here? Yeah, this is another quote, a gospel quote from Matthew. We talked about the Matthew principle. This is a very strange injunction. "Ask and it will be given to you. Seek and you'll find. Knock and it shall be opened unto you." All right, we're going to think about that for a minute. one of the things you might ask yourself is, what is it exactly that you're doing when you're thinking? you're thinking about something serious that has to do with you. imagine what you have to do to actually think seriously about something. the first thing you have to do is, you have to admit that you have a problem or you don't know something. the search has to begin with an admission of error or insufficiency. Something isn't right, and I don't know. that's a gesture of humility. You could think about that as an opening up. It's like you have a question in mind. . And then, then you seem to be able to think up an answer. Now, not always. And maybe you have to discuss it with other people. Maybe you have to do some reading and some investigation. But weirdly enough, how the hell does this work? If you ask yourself a question, there's some probability you'll get an answer, and there's even some probability that you'll get the right answer. And you thought that up. But that begs the question—it's like, how do you do that exactly? What do you mean, you thought that up? Because you don't know how you did that. It's more like you ask yourself a question, and the answer makes itself known. And you might attribute that to yourself. But then you have to ask, if you could do it yourself, why do you have the problem to begin with? Why do you have to ask the question? If you had the knowledge at hand, why was it a mystery? And if it was a mystery, then, why was it a mystery? And if it was a mystery, then where the hell did the answer come from? One of the things Jung said, and I think this is right, is that although people don't really notice this, it's like, thoughts that appear in the landscape of your imagination are like walking into a room and noticing that there's furniture there. You do the noticing, but you don't know how it got there. It's a given in some ways. And I think, I believe, that I believe that thought is literally secularized prayer. Because the prayer concept was, the prayer and atonement concept was, you had to admit there was something wrong with you, and you had to open yourself up to a revelation. Then you had to assess the quality of the revelation. And I think that's exactly what you do when you think, except if you're secular, you attribute the consequences of the thought to yourself, whatever that means. But like I said, that gets you into those philosophical conundrums that I just laid out. If you could think it up, how did you do that? Because you certainly don't know. And if it was within your power to do that thinking, that spontaneous creative act, which you don't understand, why did you have to do it? Why do you have the problem to begin with? And where'd the new information come from? It's not like we know the answer to any of these questions, but we should be smart enough to know we don't know the answer, and it's quite—I think it's a revelation fundamentally, and you experience it that way because now and then, you ask yourself a difficult question. Maybe you don't really want to, and you actually want the answer, which is also terrifying because most of the time, if you ask yourself a difficult question, you're not going to get the answer you want. You might get the answer you need. It'll be something that points to something that's insufficient about you that you need to change, generally speaking, or to a blind spot you have in a relationship or something like that. Generally, you have a sense of how true what you think up is by how much you wish it wasn't the case, and that's a very interesting thing to note, too. Anyways, you approach the mystery on your knees. I need some help. And if you're fortunate, it arrives, and that's frequently the case. Sometimes it'll appear in the form of a fantasy or dream, which is why dreams can be analyzed in psychotherapy with some utility, if you're fortunate enough to find someone who has the perspicacity necessary to analyze a dream. It's a very difficult thing to do. The dream is a proto-thought. A dream is a place where thoughts emerge, and the dream is a mystery because it's the thought before it's absolutely clear; it's the first stages of the process by which things you don't understand at all start to become yours. And the dream is mysterious not because it's trying to wrap up something you've repressed in a mystery to hide itself from you, but because the dream is the best first-pass approximation solution to the problem that you've presented. Part of the reason that you're dreaming at night is because you're trying to reorganize the way you look at the world, underneath the explicit and the semantics, that you can adapt yourself more particularly to the structure of the world. That works, whether you remember the dreams or not, . But if you do remember them and you can interpret them, sometimes you can jump the adaptation process forward and it's not that mysterious in some ways. imagine this and say, imagine we did this as an exercise. Say, I want you to think about one way your life could be better in a year that would be relevant to you, that you think would be attainable. now, to do that, you have to set that question up in your mind. It's like, what, what's one thing I'm unhappy about? Do I have some vision of how that might be improved and what might reasonably be expected in a year? now you close your eyes and then you let yourself, think about it. what does that mean? Think about it in words. Or more likely, you could generate an image that's like the daydreaming that a child engages in—and that daydreaming, that's a waking dream. It'll be in images, like a moving picture. moving picture, a movie is actually a collective dream. That's another way of thinking about it. And the birthplace of your hypothesis about what your better future could be will make itself manifest in the form of a vision. Literally. And people have visions all the time. It isn't how we describe them. When you're reading a book, a novel, the characters come to life in your imagination. That's a vision. When you daydream, that's a vision. It's a form of thought. But it's also a form of revelation, partly because—why revelation? it has an autonomy, and this. If you fantasize, if you fantasize sexually, there'll be a part of that that's voluntary. You set up the image, but it'll play itself out as if it has its own autonomy, its own characterization. People who write novels report this all the time. They don't know what the hell is going to happen to the characters. The story unfolds in their imagination. They capture it in words. There's an in-built dynamism that's autonomous in the fantasy. And one of the reasons that people have a religious impulse, is because they've noted over millennia that process of fantastic approach to the solution of problems has an autonomy. what would you say? It's characterized by a spirit that's not exactly you, in the same way that your conscience isn't exactly you, or in the same way that things that grip your interest aren't exactly you. Jung, when he talked about the collective unconscious, his hypothesis was that the deeper reaches of the collective unconscious constituted the spirit that makes itself manifest in everyone, that generates the fantasies that constitute the initial solutions to the problems of life. it's tied deep down into the instinctual substrate, and there is an autonomy to that. And Jung's proposition was that the entity that people regard as God is the concretization of that autonomy of spiritual development. Brilliant, a brilliant hypothesis. I also think that one that's irrefutable. back to this statement. Ask and it shall be given to you. what does this mean? It means that you actually have to ask. this has never worked for me. It's like, first of all, that's not true because you think, and now and then that works. And you might ask yourself, how could you think if you were really thinking? And really thinking might be, "I'm asking a dead serious question here, and I'm willing to accept any answer whatsoever, as long as I find it credible and motivating, no matter what I have to give up." And that's a sacrificial gesture. And maybe you're very unhappy in your marriage and you're trying to figure out why and you think, "Oh my God, I'm at the end of my bloody rope. I'll do anything to fix this." And then you have a fantasy, and God only knows what that is. And if you don't do that, maybe it'll be a murderous fantasy because that's when the problem-solving mechanism has been suppressed enough and lied about enough to start to become seriously pathological. You might want to consult yourself with a little bit more regularity before it comes to that. But the fantasy will make itself manifest and there'll be things that you have to change. And those are parts of you that you—parts of you that you have to let die. And that's part of the pain of thought, and it's part of the pain of genuine conversation with people. Because maybe you're sitting down with your wife trying to sort through what the hell went wrong, and you find out that there's parts of you, buddy, they really have to go. And those might be like limbs, not just like fragments of your being, whole parts of you that have to burn away. God, it's no wonder people don't want to do that. But, how do you put yourself in a position where you're willing to ask? I would say, one of the things you can do is you could use some terror on your side. here's something to contemplate. You can try this. It's interesting. You might have to practice it a bit before you get good at it. imagine you sat down and you allowed yourself to think about all the stupid things you do that are stupid. There's going to be things you do you don't know. And maybe it's because you're blind or you're ignorant or whatever, but there's some things you're doing for sure that are stupid. And there are also some of those things that you could stop doing, but for whatever reason, don't. And then you might think, imagine I let those things have free rein. I just stop resisting them. I let them take me wherever the hell they're actually aiming. What would that look like five years down the road? Now, everyone's temperament predisposes them to a different domain of temptation. for example, if you look at narcissistic people, narcissistic people want unearned attention and they want unearned status, ? And then what are the personality predictors of narcissism? And if you're extroverted and disagreeable, you're more likely to be narcissistic. And then you might think about that as a form of genetic determinism, because whether you're extroverted is like 50% genetic, and whether you're disagreeable is 50% genetic. And that seems to indicate that whether or not you're narcissistic has a genetic element and a powerful one. And then it's deterministic and—but then, how do you wrestle with a problem like that? And one of the answers to that is, I don't care what your temperament is. It's going to confer on you a set of advantages, but it's also going to confer on you a set of probable disadvantages. And that'll be the temptations that beckon to you. I studied people who were prone to alcoholism, and they were often people who had multi-generational family histories of alcoholism. And if you gave these people alcohol, their heart rate would go up like 30% after four drinks. And it was because they were responding to alcohol as if it was a cocaine-like, actually an opiate-like psychomotor stimulant. And lots of people don't respond to alcohol like that at all. But if you do, you're really going to enjoy alcohol. And you can see that there's a biological component to that. You might think, that's radically unfair. And I suppose it is, but it's more complicated than that because your temperament might tilt you towards antisocial behavior, criminality, or narcissism. But it also might tilt you towards, like, sexual licentiousness or neuroticism or depression or anxiety. There's going to be a genetic proclivity to some domain of sin for you. But that doesn't mean precisely that it's deterministic. It just means that some things are going to be more tempting for you than others, and you're going to have to wrestle with those things. And other people have to wrestle too, but maybe with different temptations. that's a good way of thinking about that. And you might even be strongly tempted in a particular direction because of your temperament. You're hyper-extroverted and you're hyper-disagreeable, narcissism is really going to be a temptation. What's the advantage? if you're really extroverted, you have all the advantages of being really extroverted. You're charismatic and dynamic. You like being around other people. You have a lot of energy. You have a lot of positive emotion. And if you're disagreeable, it's bloody difficult for people to take advantage of you. But if you're charismatic and it's difficult to take advantage of you, it's quite easy to take advantage of other people. It's like, you can't get the advantages without the disadvantages. And then maybe you can be wise enough, if you're bloody likely and careful, lucky and careful, to regulate the temptation and manage to capitalize, on the advantages. back to contemplation. Most people know what hell they would end up in if they allowed themselves to go in that direction. Some people can't control their temper. Some people can't control their drug intake. Some people can't control their despair or their appetite. Who the hell knows where you'd end up if you allowed yourself to fall apart. But you probably have some idea. then, one of the things you can do is, play it out. Imagine what you've done that was stupid in the past, that hurt you. There's probably a pattern of some sort there because people tend to have their pattern of errors. And then you can think, you stop resisting that. You let it take you over completely. What hell are you in, in five years? And maybe you're, I don't know, maybe you're on crank in downtown Portland, bent over. That's you. Is that really what you want? And you've got to think it through. Not like some abstraction, but like some deeply embodied fantasy. And you got to think, how much do I not want that, and how probable is that, and do I even want to taste it that. Or maybe I just want not to go there at all. And the more real you make it—when you're getting people to expose themselves to things they're afraid of and avoiding, and you get them to do that in their imagination, the more real they make the imagination, which you can measure by measuring their psychophysiological responses. Because if you have a frightening fantasy and it's real, you'll sweat more. And that can be measured. The more realistic people make the fantasy, the faster they progress in exposure therapy. And you can do this with your daydream. It's like, what would you be like if you were as bad as you could be? In the particularized way that you would be the worst you could be? You might think, I'd never do that. you should disabuse yourself that thought very, very rapidly. Because that's actually one of the things I learned about totalitarianism. It's the people who think they would be least likely to follow the dictates of a totalitarian regime that are in fact the most likely to be exactly those people. It's like, no, it's probably you, buddy. If you can't see it, it just means you're blind. And this is partly, actually, a grappling with your capability for malevolence, for aiming down. And you can be sure there's things in you that are aiming down. And no, why would I aim down? It's like, ah, you're bitter. How would that be? You've been betrayed, you're resentful, you want revenge on other people or maybe yourself, or maybe you want revenge on God for making such a godforsaken reality to begin with. I mean, people have these motivations. If you don't see them, you're not paying attention. And you should pay attention because those motivations, first of all, they get in your way. And second, they might divert you. But even perhaps more importantly, if you get them behind you, pushing you forward, they make you very difficult to stop. If you let your fear stop you, then you're stopped. But if your fear is propelling you, you're a lot more difficult an agent to interfere with. And you think—one of the reasons, I don't know if this is a good example but it might be. I got myself in trouble about seven years ago for saying some things that people thought I shouldn't say, and the reason I said them was because I was much more afraid of the consequences of losing control of my tongue than I was afraid of whatever the hell the idiot administrators at the university were going to manage to array against me. You've got to know what to be afraid of. And one of the things you should be afraid of is your own capacity for self-destructive stupidity. And you can play that out. You think, there's a hell I don't think I'm going to visit. But you have to make it real and you have to make it personal, and that's a frightening thing.

title: Plan - 5. Faith in Tragedy
content: The Christian Passion story nests at the bottom of our culture. And there's a reason for that. It's necessarily the case. And Jung called that story an archetypal tragedy. And this is what he meant by that. It's like the story in the Book of Job. the Book of Job is a story about a good man. God even admits he's good. And God makes a bet with Satan. And Satan comes along and has a chat with God and says, "You think Job is good, but I don't think . I think he's just fortunate. If you stripped him of everything about his life that would be good, he would become bitter and turn against himself and turn against you." And God says, "Yeah, I don't think ." And Satan says, "why don't you let me have at him and find out?" And God says, "Yes," which is rather a bitter thing for God to do. But there will be definitely times in your life where you feel exactly like that's what's happened to you. And what happens to Job is that almost everything that could possibly be terrible that could happen to a person happens to him. And the story is about how he contends with that. It's a tragedy and an archetypal tragedy. you might think, what's a tragedy? life is a tragedy. There's tragic aspects to life. And what's a tragedy? Tragedy is when a terrible thing happens to someone. But that can be justice. If you go to a movie and a terrible thing happens to an arch-criminal, you're actually happy about it. You don't think it's a tragedy. it's not merely that terrible things happen. It's that terrible things happen in an unjust way. That's a tragedy. And then you might think, what's the ultimate tragedy? And the ultimate tragedy is when the worst possible thing happens to the least possibly deserving person, right? And the reason that story is at the basis of our culture is because you're going to have to contend with that at some point in your life, because there will be things that will happen to you, despite your innocence, at least in that regard, that make you suffer dreadfully. And if it doesn't happen to you, it'll happen to your children, which is a situation that makes it even more poignant and terrible. And you have to contend with the problem of unjust suffering. And the archetypal story sits at the bottom of our culture because everyone has to contend with that. The Christian Passion is not only the wrestling with tragedy, an unjust tragedy, it's also the harrowing of hell. Part of the mythological dream that surrounds the canonical Judeo-Christian story is that after Christ is crucified, he descends into hell. Think, what does that mean psychologically, ? And what it means is, not only will you have to—every soul has to confront the reality of tragedy and unjust suffering, but that you have to also confront the reality of malevolence. And maybe that's even worse than death. When you look at soldiers who develop post-traumatic stress disorder, most of the time they don't develop that because something terrible has happened to them.
